articles.title: North Korea Fires Ballistic Missiles, Deepening Silence Fuels Analyst Speculation
articles.full_text:
Seoul, Tokyo, and Washington condemned two ballistic missile launches ahead of allied military drills, but Pyongyang’s failure to report either test has left analysts guessing at the cause.
This file photo provided by North Korean state media shows the launch of one of the five Hwasongpho-11 Ra missiles tested on April 19, 2026. North Korea has not yet provided images of the launches in August 2026.
North Korea fired what appeared to be a midrange ballistic missile toward the ocean east of the peninsula on August 12, its second launch in less than a week, according to South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS). 
The back-to-back launches came two days after South Korea and the United States announced their plans for joint drills. The annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise is set to begin on August 17. The allies describe the drills as defensive. but North Korea has for years denounced them as invasion rehearsals and has frequently responded with weapons tests timed around the training period. 
The missile lifted off from the Wonsan area on North Korea’s east coast around 6 a.m. and flew more than 700 kilometers, or about 435 miles, before falling into the sea. Authorities in South Korea, the United States, and Japan tracked the launch from its early stages and were still analyzing its exact specifications as of this writing. The JCS did not disclose the missile’s type or flight angle, a departure from its usual practice of offering at least a preliminary classification within hours of a launch. By South Korea’s count, it was Pyongyang’s 11th ballistic missile launch of 2026.
The test followed a shorter-range ballistic missile that North Korea fired from the same Wonsan area on August 6. That earlier test was Pyongyang’s first ballistic weapons test in 48 days, breaking a lull that had persisted since its missile launch on June 25. Kim Jong Un, the autocratic leader of North Korea, was shown new missile systems that day, including a modular launcher developed as an analogue of the U.S. HIMARS rocket system.
South Korea’s presidential national security office convened emergency meetings after both launches, calling them provocations that violate United Nations Security Council resolutions and urging Pyongyang to halt such tests immediately. Officials said the military would maintain readiness to respond to any further provocation in coordination with the United States. 
The Japanese government also protested both launches. Defense Minister Koizumi Shinjiro told reporters the missile landed outside Japan’s exclusive economic zone. He added that Tokyo had lodged a protest with Pyongyang through diplomatic channels in Beijing. Koizumi described the repeated launches as “a threat to the peace and security of Japan, the region, and the international community.”
The foreign ministries of South Korea, the United States, and Japan also held a trilateral telephone call after the August 12 launch, where they “reaffirmed that ballistic missile launches by North Korea violate the relevant U.N. Security Council Resolutions and called on North Korea to cease such provocations that threaten the peace and security of the region and the international community.”
The U.S. Pacific Command said after both launches that it was consulting closely with allies and partners. That assessment found no immediate threat to U.S. personnel, territory, or allies, and it reaffirmed Washington’s defense commitment to the region. 
North Korea has tested ballistic missiles regularly since the collapse of nuclear talks between Kim and U.S. President Donald Trump in 2019, expanding an arsenal barred under multiple U.N. Security Council resolutions. Wonsan, on the east coast, has become one of the launch sites North Korea uses most often. Firing toward the eastern ocean lets the military test range and altitude without sending debris over South Korean, Japanese, or Chinese territory. That geographic reality has made the area a default choice for routine tests. 
The KN-23, part of North Korea’s short-range arsenal, is a solid-fuel missile modeled on the Iskander system built in Russia, with a maximum range of roughly 700 to 800 kilometers, close to the distance reported for the August 12 launch. However, South Korean officials said they needed more time to identify the type of missile fired on August 12. 
The JCS’s unusual reticence about its range and angle points to something beyond a routine short-range test. According to local media reports, the missile tested on August 6 showed flight characteristics that differed from a conventional ballistic trajectory. That raised the possibility North Korea tested the gliding profile of a short-range hypersonic system before firing a related missile to near-maximum range six days later.
North Korea has not confirmed the launches at all, much less which specific missile was involved.
Kim ordered a 2.5-fold increase in ballistic and cruise missile production during a visit to a missile industrial facility in early June and state media have since highlighted new systems such as the Hwasal-2 cruise missile and a submarine-launched variant called the Pulhwasal-3-31. The August 12 launch thus extended a pattern that has intensified since Kim ordered the scale-up in missile production. 
Pyongyang has also deepened military cooperation with Russia amid the war in Ukraine, giving it added incentive to keep testing and refining its missile inventory even outside politically charged periods such as joint allied drills.
Seen against that backdrop, the resumption of launches after the June 25 test looks less like an isolated reaction to any single event and more like a continuation of a production and testing cycle Kim set in motion earlier in the summer. The timing around Ulchi Freedom Shield gave Pyongyang an opportunity to fold a routine test into a familiar cycle of protest, not the other way around.
Although North Korea seems to be focusing on developing its missile systems regardless of external actions, it does not mean the political calendar was incidental. The launch came within days of the announcement of Ulchi Freedom Shield. Pyongyang has a habit of pairing weapons development with a message of defiance toward Seoul and Washington. A single launch can serve both purposes, advancing a weapons program while reminding the allies that Pyongyang can respond to their exercises.
North Korea typically confirms major missile tests through state media such as the Korean Central News Agency within a day, usually describing them as successful demonstrations of its defense capabilities. Neither launch had been acknowledged by North Korean media as of August 13, an unusual gap given Pyongyang’s normal pattern of disclosure.
However, state media has not reported on every test. North Korea has previously stayed silent about tests that it later described as routine work by its Missile Administration and affiliated defense science institutes, unrelated to regional developments. In light of that, the silence around this week’s launches is consistent with tests folded into a preset development schedule rather than a public messaging campaign. 
The launches may have involved a still-developing weapons system that Pyongyang is not ready to unveil yet. In local media reports, the lack of disclosure has also fed speculation that one or both tests may have failed. 
With Ulchi Freedom Shield set to kick off, officials in Seoul and Tokyo are watching for additional launches during the drills – a period when Pyongyang has historically stepped up weapons tests to underscore its objections. Whether North Korea eventually breaks its silence on the recent ballistic missile launches may itself send a signal. It could show whether the launches were meant as routine progress on the missile program, a political statement aimed at the allies, or both at once. 
North Korea fired what appeared to be a midrange ballistic missile toward the ocean east of the peninsula on August 12, its second launch in less than a week, according to South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS). 
The back-to-back launches came two days after South Korea and the United States announced their plans for joint drills. The annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise is set to begin on August 17. The allies describe the drills as defensive. but North Korea has for years denounced them as invasion rehearsals and has frequently responded with weapons tests timed around the training period. 
The missile lifted off from the Wonsan area on North Korea’s east coast around 6 a.m. and flew more than 700 kilometers, or about 435 miles, before falling into the sea. Authorities in South Korea, the United States, and Japan tracked the launch from its early stages and were still analyzing its exact specifications as of this writing. The JCS did not disclose the missile’s type or flight angle, a departure from its usual practice of offering at least a preliminary classification within hours of a launch. By South Korea’s count, it was Pyongyang’s 11th ballistic missile launch of 2026.
The test followed a shorter-range ballistic missile that North Korea fired from the same Wonsan area on August 6. That earlier test was Pyongyang’s first ballistic weapons test in 48 days, breaking a lull that had persisted since its missile launch on June 25. Kim Jong Un, the autocratic leader of North Korea, was shown new missile systems that day, including a modular launcher developed as an analogue of the U.S. HIMARS rocket system.
South Korea’s presidential national security office convened emergency meetings after both launches, calling them provocations that violate United Nations Security Council resolutions and urging Pyongyang to halt such tests immediately. Officials said the military would maintain readiness to respond to any further provocation in coordination with the United States. 
The Japanese government also protested both launches. Defense Minister Koizumi Shinjiro told reporters the missile landed outside Japan’s exclusive economic zone. He added that Tokyo had lodged a protest with Pyongyang through diplomatic channels in Beijing. Koizumi described the repeated launches as “a threat to the peace and security of Japan, the region, and the international community.”
The foreign ministries of South Korea, the United States, and Japan also held a trilateral telephone call after the August 12 launch, where they “reaffirmed that ballistic missile launches by North Korea violate the relevant U.N. Security Council Resolutions and called on North Korea to cease such provocations that threaten the peace and security of the region and the international community.”
The U.S. Pacific Command said after both launches that it was consulting closely with allies and partners. That assessment found no immediate threat to U.S. personnel, territory, or allies, and it reaffirmed Washington’s defense commitment to the region.
articles.summary: Seoul, Tokyo, and Washington condemned two ballistic missile launches ahead of allied military drills, but Pyongyang’s failure to report either test has left analysts guessing at the cause.

articles.title: The US Military Can’t Function Without China
articles.full_text:
Rare earths are critical to making modern weapons – and China dominates the supply chain.
A U.S. Air Force F-35A Lightning II aircraft receives fuel from a U.S. Air Force KC-135 Stratotanker aircraft in the U.S. Central Command area of responsibility Aug. 8, 2026.
The manufacture of modern weapons begins with complex materials, especially those containing rare earth elements. These elements are used to make everything from magnets and sensors to radars and lasers. According to the U.S. Department of Defense, an F-35 fighter requires more than 400 kilograms of rare earths to build; a destroyer and submarine, respectively, can require anywhere from two to five metric tons. Rare earths also appear in Tomahawk missiles, Predator drones, and the many missiles and bombs that have been used in Iran over the last few months. 
The problem for the U.S. military is that China accounts for roughly 70 percent of all rare earth mining and more than 90 percent of all rare earth processing, dominating entire categories of critical materials needed to make semiconductors, avionics, batteries, and things that go boom. According to the U.S. Geological Survey, China leads global production in 30 of 44 critical minerals while maintaining, in each of those 30 minerals, at least one monopoly in mining, refining, or processing.
Of the many components employed in modern military manufacturing, rare earth magnets are among the most important. Neodymium magnets are prized for being able to produce enormous magnetic forces relative to their low mass, making them invaluable for motors and guidance systems, where every bit of additional weight or electricity consumption can bring debilitating inefficiencies. Supplementing with other rare earths like dysprosium or terbium can make these magnets retain performance at high temperatures while adding samarium and cobalt can enhance stability under pressure, especially useful when flying things at high velocities. In 2025, China mined an estimated 270,000 metric tons of these elements out of a global total of 390,000 tons, accounting for roughly 69 percent of the world’s extraction. 
Samarium is probably one of the most important rare earths you have never heard of. It is a critical component used in everything from chemical manufacturing and cancer treatment to nuclear reactors and satellites – and Chinese companies essentially hold a monopoly on all of the world’s samarium processing. Following tariff tensions with Washington at the start of U.S. President Donald Trump’s second term in 2025, Beijing restricted samarium exports for military applications, forcing American weapons manufacturers to search for alternative sources. Most were unable to locate these alternatives. One highly publicized exception was the lucky acquisition of a long-forgotten cache in France, and that still resulted in processing expenses over five times that of the typical Chinese export.
Beyond rare earths, China controls the production of other critical minerals – like tungsten, which is also currently under Chinese export control. Its exceptional density, hardness, and heat resistance make it ideal for armor-piercing applications and radiation shielding, especially in nuclear submarines. Perhaps more importantly, tungsten is indispensable for making the basic cutting and drilling tools required throughout military fabrication: tools necessary to make everything from bullets and tanks to helicopters and battleships. China produces over 80 percent of the world’s tungsten. When Chinese exports of the element fell by almost 40 percent year on year after Beijing’s export controls took effect, prices skyrocketed amid the scarcity.
Following China’s initial export controls in April of 2025, the United States and European Union were quick to reach preliminary agreements to restart critical mineral exports. Trade tensions lingered, however, resulting in Beijing eventually extending export controls to other elements and even the sale of mineral processing equipment. Some of these controls were subsequently delayed, but the basic requirement for Chinese exporters to carefully vet foreign buyers and reject sales destined for military applications has largely remained in effect since 2025. That essentially shuts American weapons manufacturers out of direct access to Chinese rare earth materials and the high-tech products resulting from them.
Given that most manufacturers tend to have some raw materials on hand at any given time, there has been a noticeable lag between the market disruptions illustrated above and tangible adverse outcomes in production. Many of these downstream outcomes are just starting to be reported now, over a year after the export controls began. A recent batch of new F-35s, for example, was reportedly delivered without their AN/APG-85 radars, rendering the planes unusable in combat and only suitable for limited training exercises. Similar delays in the manufacture of combat-ready drones have also been reported, usually attributed to the spiking cost of samarium, which has been reported to be offered at prices up to 60 times the pre-control average. The shortage of even one critical rare earth component can render a $100 million machine essentially useless.
The United States’ recent conflict with Iran has added even more urgency to these supply chain issues. After five months of extensive aerial activity, the U.S. has reportedly expended “virtually all” of its available ATACMS and Precision Strike Missiles, along with roughly half of its Tomahawk cruise missiles, and substantial portions of its Patriot and THAAD interceptors. All of these require extensive quantities of rare earth components to replenish. In response, the Pentagon has pressured weapons manufacturers to accelerate production, signing agreements intended to triple production for Patriot components and quadruple it for THAAD. It remains to be seen, however, whether already-strained supply chains will be able to accommodate these desired surges in production.
Washington has, of course, not been oblivious to these rare earth supply problems. In July 2025, the Pentagon agreed to invest $400 million in MP Materials, operator of the only active rare earth mine in the United States. The investment package included a $150 million loan, a commitment to purchase output from a planned magnet factory, and price guarantees intended to help American producers compete with Chinese exports. A year later, the Pentagon announced a similar $25 million investment in ReElement Technologies to expand domestic processing of critical minerals, most notably gallium and germanium. 
Washington has also pursued partnerships with mineral-rich allies in an effort to diversify rare earth supply. In October of 2025, for example, the United States and Australia committed a combined $3 billion to critical mineral mining and processing projects, including measures intended to support alternative supply chains outside of China. The U.S. has likewise invested more than $70 million in Canadian mineral projects through the Defense Production Act, as part of its multinational Minerals Security Partnership launched in 2022.
Partnerships and money, of course, are only the first steps to getting new mines up and running. New mine construction in the U.S. typically takes an average of 29 years to complete, due to the extensive amounts of time required for surveying, permits, planning, and infrastructure expansion. Once a mine becomes operational, processing facilities are then needed to refine the extracted ores. These latter facilities need to be scaled appropriately to produce finished materials of consistent quality and in sufficient quantities at operational margins that can turn a profit even when put into competition with Chinese companies, many of which are now widely regarded as world leaders. Simply put, investments alone guarantee nothing, with any returns on investment potentially being realized only many, many years later, a common deterrent to the investment of commercial capital in these areas.
Finished rare earths, of course, do not automatically become magnetics and semiconductors either. With China being responsible for producing over 90 percent of the world’s rare earth magnets, it remains unclear how the U.S. military industrial complex will be able to produce or procure the high-tech components it needs at scale without Chinese exports, even if refined components were miraculously made available domestically in the short term. Appropriate financing and long-term investment would, again, be integral components to any solution but it remains unclear whether the United States even has the required technical expertise or sufficient numbers of skilled workers available to build and operate the many different facilities that would be required to mine, refine, process, and then actually build the magnets, alloys, and other products needed. 
How long American F-35s will continue to go without their radars is anybody’s guess.

articles.title: Can Japan’s Defense Industry Meet its Ambitious Goals?
articles.full_text:
Japan increasingly recognizes the importance of the defense industrial base as a source of strategic capability. But can the industry actually deliver?
MHI launched Tatsuta, the eleventh Mogami-class frigate on order for the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force, in a ceremony held at its facilities in Nagasaki, Japan, July 2, 2025.
On August 4, the Japanese Ministry of Defense published its annual 2026 Defense White Paper, which outlines Japan’s defense policies and activities. While the report extensively covers the increasingly severe security environment surrounding Japan, notable highlights include an emphasis on one of Japan’s core concepts, “new ways of defense,” and its defense production.  
Notably, the White Paper follows Japanese Defense Minister Koizumi Shinjiro’s comment at the Farnborough International Airshow: “Defense production is deterrence itself. No matter how advanced a defense system may be, it means little if it cannot be produced.” His statement suggests a fundamental shift in how Japan views deterrence: rather than mere possession of defense materiel, Japan increasingly recognizes the importance of the defense industrial base as a source of strategic capability.   
Japan, like other countries around the world, is learning from Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Some of the takeaways include the decisive role played by unmanned assets, renewed appreciation for strong air defense, and the importance of sustaining a defense industrial base that can keep up with a protracted war. Furthermore, recent conflict in the Middle East and concerns about diminishing U.S. stockpiles have sparked concern among U.S. allies about the reliability of the United States as a supplier of advanced munitions for their militaries. These conflicts have served as critical turning points in Japan’s defense posture, prompting the Japanese government to rethink its defense policies to invest more in developing indigenous capabilities and partner with other U.S. allies that share similar concerns.   
Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae’s administration is expected to complete the revision of Japan’s three key security documents by the end of 2026. The updates are anticipated to reorient Japan’s national security strategy to better respond to the aggravating regional security environment, integrate new capabilities with strengthened alliances and partnerships, and develop greater self-reliance. Takaichi has already made notable progress in strengthening Japan’s security posture, including the relaxation of the Implementation Guidelines for the Three Principles on Transfer of Defense Equipment and Technology, lifting a long-standing ban on lethal weapons exports. 
The revision, which opened the door for Japan to export lethal weapons to 17 countries that have signed the Equipment and Technology Transfer Agreements (ETTAs), was done with the goal of strengthening Japan’s relations with its allies while contributing to the country’s economic growth through a stronger defense industrial base. Japan has already signed a $7 billion contract with Australia to deliver Mogami-class frigates beginning in 2029 and begun discussions with the government of the Philippines to export Type 88 surface-to-ship missiles. While visiting Singapore to attend the Shangri-La Dialogue in May, Koizumi also engaged in the discussion of the potential sale of Mogami-class frigates with his New Zealand counterpart. 
With the new guidelines, Japan will be able to export weapons that were developed under joint production to third countries. That includes the Global Combat Air Program (GCAP) – the trilateral six-generation fighter development program that unites Japan, Italy, and the United Kingdom. Now, Canada has joined the GCAP as an observer.  
However, as the Defense White Paper points out, there are multiple factors that Japan must improve to build a strong indigenous industrial base. For example, to ensure efficient production of domestic defense capabilities, Japan must shore up its supply chain resilience. Like other countries around the world, Japan is vulnerable to critical material shortages due to global conflicts and restrictions placed by countries. Japan also needs to improve its manufacturing efficiency and strengthen its cybersecurity. Finally, Japan will need to maintain business management and training personnel in the defense industry. This is a significant challenge for Japan, which is experiencing labor shortages due to its aging society. 
In addition, Japan faces challenges with companies reducing their defense business or withdrawing from the defense market altogether. The Ministry of Defense and the Japanese government must make defense production more attractive to companies so that they can strengthen production.   
With a stronger defense industrial base, Japan can increase its autonomy and also contribute to greater alliance relationship building with the United States and key partners. The ambitious goals that Japan has set require more than just an increase in defense spending, however. Ultimately, without the basic requirement of having enough companies and labor involved in defense production, Tokyo’s long-term goal will be impossible to reach. 
As Japan continues to revise its key security documents, it is critical that the Japanese government and Ministry of Defense realistically assess their industrial capabilities and maintain a long-term focus and commitment to strengthening and sustaining its defense industrial base.

articles.title: Competing Interests, Common Narrative: How Industry Shapes the AI Race
articles.full_text:
Different firms in the AI value chain invoke the AI race narrative, but with different policy preferences in mind.
A recent Wall Street Journal article warned that the “[c]lampdown on top U.S. artificial intelligence is fueling concern that Washington is handing Beijing a cyberwarfare advantage.” It went on to note that China’s release of Z.ai by Zhipu AI is on par with Anthropic’s Mythos model in detecting software vulnerabilities. The article, along with a growing body of recent commentary, taps into the prevailing China-U.S. AI race narrative at a time when the United States is deliberating a unified AI policy and reportedly considering banning Chinese open weight models. 
The AI race narrative holds that the United States and China are engaged in a zero-sum contest to develop and deploy frontier AI so as to accrue lasting geoeconomic advantage. In a May 2026 article for the Transformer newsletter, Yi-Ling Liu outlined how Silicon Valley’s major companies have themselves pushed this AI race narrative, potentially overstating the extent of the competition. However, the interests of these companies are not uniform, nor are the policies that they advocate. Different firms across the AI value chain have continued to invoke the AI race narrative to advance policy preferences that align with their commercial interests.  
Given the concentrated nature of the global AI supply chain, a select few companies have immense stakes in how policies and regulations on AI evolve and, consequently, strong incentives to shape them. Sitting atop the hardware segment of the AI supply chain is Nvidia, which accounts for over 80 percent of global AI chip sales. Nvidia’s GPUs form the backbone of the compute infrastructure required to train and develop generative AI models. This market position, while enviable, has exposed Nvidia to the broader geoeconomic disruptions that have emanated from the AI race with China. 
In April 2025, building on Biden-era export controls, the Trump administration introduced measures that would require Nvidia to secure additional export licenses for the sale of its H20 chips to China, which would result in a $5.5 billion accounting charge. In response, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang extensively lobbied the administration to reverse this policy and reconsider its broader approach toward the export of AI chips to China. 
As part of this effort, Nvidia skillfully invoked the AI race narrative to achieve its objective. In a report presented to the government, the company argued that existing chip restrictions would only accelerate Huawei’s production of indigenous alternatives, increase its market share, and pave the way for the company to eventually become a competitive threat, thus eroding U.S. technological leadership in AI. While the basis for these claims is contested, it proved to be effective in convincing the Trump administration to relax its export control policy, enabling Nvidia to resume sales to China. The Trump administration’s decision to permit H20 exports was reportedly linked to a trade deal for rare earths from China. The subsequent policy shift allowing for the export of more advanced H200 chips, in limited quantities, can be understood as part of Nvidia’s broader lobbying campaign.
Beyond hardware, American companies also currently lead the development and deployment of closed-source proprietary AI models. In contrast, Chinese companies have developed and deployed open-weight models that are fast closing this performance gap and offering lower cost alternatives. This progress is driven by a range of factors, including AI model distillation – a method that involves transferring knowledge from larger AI models to smaller, faster, and cheaper models. Companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI have accused Chinese AI developers of using distillation to reproduce the capabilities of proprietary models. In a recent press release, Anthropic claimed that three Chinese AI labs were involved in an industrial scale campaign to extract capabilities from Claude, necessitating a coordinated response from “industry players, policy makers, and the global AI community.” More notably, Anthropic highlighted its consistent support of “export controls to help maintain America’s lead in AI” and argued that such distillation attempts by Chinese labs “reinforce the rationale for export controls.” 
While the legality of distillation is beyond the scope of this article, it is pertinent to examine Anthropic’s framing of the incident. By portraying distillation attempts by Chinese AI laboratories as akin to industrial intellectual property theft, Anthropic has positioned its AI models as strategic assets in the ongoing AI race that require regulatory protection and, if necessary, punitive enforcement by the U.S. government. As Craig Smith aptly noted, “Anthropic’s larger project is to persuade Washington to define the rules of the frontier so that model extraction becomes a sanctionable offense.” 
Recent developments in Washington indicate that Anthropic’s efforts for such a policy shift may be gaining traction. In a recent tweet, Director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy Michael Krastios referenced Chinese AI Lab Moonshot’s efforts to distill from Anthropic’s Fable to develop its K3 model using sophisticated means. He also reiterated the U.S. commitment to fostering a competitive ecosystem for AI development, while stressing that “large-scale, covert industrial distillation aimed at stealing proprietary U.S. technology and undermining American research is unacceptable” – echoing concerns previously raised by Anthropic. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent issued a similar tweet and warned that industrial-scale distillation “attacks” by China could trigger “sanctions and Entity List designations.” 
The timing of these statements is noteworthy as it comes during a period when the White House is reportedly weighing bans on Chinese open weight models. While a ban on Chinese open weight models would potentially shield companies like Anthropic from the competitive reach of their Chinese counterparts, it has elicited concern from other industry players. On July 24, Nvidia, Microsoft, Meta, and other companies signed an open letter titled “Open Weights and the American AI leadership” that urged Washington to avoid premature restrictions; cautioned policymakers not to conflate legitimate model-development techniques (distillation) with misappropriation; and advocated for an open-weight AI ecosystem as a path to sustain U.S. technology leadership. While OpenAI and Google subsequently joined the list of signatories, Anthropic remained notably absent, highlighting the divergent interests and perspectives from industry players in different segments of the AI supply chain.
Microsoft is another example where tech companies have invoked the AI race to advocate for policy change. As a provider of AI infrastructure globally, Microsoft, as well as other companies in the AI industry, expressed concerns about the potential implications of the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. In short, the AI Diffusion rule was an effort to create “a new global framework for regulating any transactions (the export, re-export, and in-country transfer) of advanced artificial intelligence (AI) model weights and high-performance computing integrated circuits.” The framework also created a three-tiered system for countries that could access this technology, placing certain import restrictions on countries that fell into the second and third tier and potentially impacting business expansion efforts of AI companies across the globe. Microsoft’s Vice Chair and President Brad Smith penned an article in February 2025 where he argued that the AI rule would undermine U.S. leadership in AI, gradually cede advantage to China in the years to come, and restrict access to vital markets. He noted:

As drafted, the rule undermines two Trump administration priorities: strengthening U.S. AI leadership and reducing the nation’s near trillion-dollar trade deficit. Left unchanged, the Biden rule will give China a strategic advantage in spreading over time its own AI technology, echoing its rapid ascent in 5G telecommunications a decade ago.     
The Trump administration ultimately rescinded the rule in May 2025 in favor of new regulations, likely in response to pushback from the tech industry. 
What stands out in these examples is how the AI race narrative was employed to serve different policy objectives. Whereas Nvidia used the narrative to advocate for modifications to U.S. export controls that would preserve its access to the Chinese market, Anthropic used a similar narrative to build a case for more stringent export controls and punitive measures to prevent Chinese labs from reproducing its AI models through distillation, thereby protecting its technological advantage and market position. Put simply, whereas Nvidia benefits from selling its hardware to multiple players in an open-weight AI ecosystem, companies such as Anthropic, whose revenues rely on the use of their proprietary models, stand to benefit from measures that safeguard their market position. Similarly, Microsoft and other technology companies have invoked this narrative to push back against regulations that impact their ability to access markets deemed crucial for their business operations. Beyond their divergent policy goals, these examples also highlight the lack of consensus among these technology companies on the AI race.  
In sum, influential companies in the global AI supply chain have a great interest in influencing and shaping evolving AI policy in the United States and have selectively deployed the AI race narrative to advocate for policies that safeguard their domestic and global market interests. As U.S. AI regulation increasingly acquires extraterritorial influence – evidenced by the recent U.S. directive to suspend access to Anthropic’s Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models – understanding how commercial actors shape these policy debates becomes essential to understanding the future of global AI governance.  
A recent Wall Street Journal article warned that the “[c]lampdown on top U.S. artificial intelligence is fueling concern that Washington is handing Beijing a cyberwarfare advantage.” It went on to note that China’s release of Z.ai by Zhipu AI is on par with Anthropic’s Mythos model in detecting software vulnerabilities. The article, along with a growing body of recent commentary, taps into the prevailing China-U.S. AI race narrative at a time when the United States is deliberating a unified AI policy and reportedly considering banning Chinese open weight models.

However, the interests of these companies are not uniform, nor are the policies that they advocate. Different firms across the AI value chain have continued to invoke the AI race narrative to advance policy preferences that align with their commercial interests.

articles.title: How the Modi Government is Downgrading India’s National Anthem
articles.full_text:
For the first time in eight decades, the country’s national song, Vande Mataram, will precede the playing of the national anthem on Independence Day.
India’s first Prime Minister, Jawaharlal Nehru, delivers the Tryst with Destiny speech inside the Indian Parliament building at midnight on August 14-15 to mark Indian independence.
On August 15, when India celebrates its Independence Day, the official celebrations from the ramparts of the Red Fort in New Delhi will, for the first time in 80 years, mark a departure from tradition. India’s national anthem “Jana Gana Mana” (The Minds of All People), which was penned by Nobel laureate Rabindranath Tagore, will be preceded by the singing of the national song, “Vande Mataram” (Hail Mother India)
Singing the national song first was a clear move by India’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government to “degrade the national anthem to a secondary status,” The Wire pointed out.
This is significant as the national anthem has constitutional status and, as per official protocol, is considered the highest musical symbol of the republic. However, the BJP and its affiliates in the Sangh Parivar have never been fond of the secular content of the national anthem and have consistently demanded primacy for the more controversial Vande Mataram, which has clear Hindu religious overtones.
Recently, the Narendra Modi government amended the law to bring Vande Mataram on par with the Jana Gana Mana. Previously, while the national anthem was played on state and ceremonial occasions, the national song was largely restricted to cultural events, and even then it was only its first two verses that were sung.
The Defense Ministry, which is in charge of the Independence Day celebrations, announced recently that “in a first,” Vande Mataram would be specially honored to commemorate the song’s 150th anniversary.
Per the new protocol, on Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s arrival at the Red Fort, the national song will be played first, the national flag will then be unfurled accompanied by the national anthem.
To the uninitiated, this may seem a needless controversy over a non-issue. It is not. It is, in fact, a part of the Sangh Parivar’s larger Hindutva agenda to replace the anthem, which celebrates India’s diversity and plurality, with the entire six stanzas of Vande Mataram, which specifically invokes the Hindu goddesses Durga, Saraswati and Lakshmi. Moreover, Vande Mataram refers to India as a Mother Goddess who is worshipped in temples.
According to the amended law, the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971, which was passed in parliament and received the president’s assent earlier this week, any insult to the national song could be punished with a three- year prison term, just as it was with the national anthem.
Unsurprisingly, Muslim organizations have opposed this imposition, arguing that it is against the basic tenets of their Islamic faith to worship anyone but Allah. In fact, even when the Modi government passed the bill with a token 15-minute debate in parliament, it was opposed by opposition MPs. K Kanimozhi, a Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) MP, lambasted the BJP for bringing in a “Hindutva agenda”  under the guise of nationalism. She said the legislation was “against federalism” and argued that nationalism could not be imposed through law.
Expectedly, the ruling BJP reiterated that the Congress-led opposition was playing “appeasement politics.” Modi has repeatedly accused the Congress party of not giving due recognition to the national song. In fact, Hindu nationalists have long accused the Congress of sowing the seeds of Partition by appeasing minorities.
The BJP’s latest move according the national song parity of status with the national anthem must be seen in the context of promoting unabashed Hindu majoritarianism.
In an earlier article on the eve of the state elections in West Bengal, I had elaborated on the BJP’s polarizing agenda in the state, with its thrust on imposition of Vande Mataram to win the votes of the Hindu majority. The BJP’s allegations against the Congress’ actions during the freedom struggle were historically inaccurate, I had pointed out.
When the Congress party, then led by Jawaharlal Nehru, consulted Tagore in 1937 on the adoption of Vande Mataram as the national song, Tagore opined that those who believe in monotheism (like Muslims, Brahmos, etc.) could find the later paragraphs objectionable as they were an invocation to the Goddess Durga. He advised Nehru to retain only the first two paragraphs of Vande Mataram as the national song for its invocation of the beauty of the motherland.
Written by the Bengali novelist Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay in 1875, Vande Mataram’s later paragraphs were incorporated in a larger version of the song in his 1882 novel, “Anandamath.”
Interestingly, it is the longer version of the song that the BJP has been championing vigorously. The 150th anniversary of Vande Mataram provided the BJP with opportunity to accelerate its campaign. The celebrations, which were kicked off last year, will reach their zenith on August 15 at Red Fort, where a floral decoration will showcase Vande Mataram and an Indian Air Force helicopter will carry a banner commemorating 150 years of Vande Mataram and shower flower petals.
Opposition-ruled states of Tamil Nadu and Kerala have already announced they will not obey the central government order. Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay announced on Wednesday that “Tamil Thaai Vazhthu,” the state’s official song, will be the first song to be sung at government events and official programs across Tamil Nadu. Tamil Thaai Vazhtu celebrates India’s long-cherished ideal of unity in diversity.
Meanwhile, the Congress government in Kerala has made it clear that all six stanzas of Vande Mataram will not be sung. The protocol of previous years of singing only the first two stanzas will be followed at all events, including Independence Day celebrations in the state.
Since it came to power in 2014, the BJP has been recasting the official Independence Day celebrations in its majoritarian vision by promoting a pro-Hindu brand of nationalism and patriotism. The Har Ghar Tiranga (The Indian Tricolor atop every house) campaign is held for an entire week in the run-up to Independence Day. The central government has integrated this with the Vande Mataram celebrations, making its singing mandatory at all national flag events.
Analysts have observed that the “Tiranga” (Tricolor) campaign is a brand of jingoism, where the thrust is on performative patriotism, not on adherence to constitutional principles of secularism, democracy and federalism.
Since 2014, the government has emphasized Hindu nationalist symbolism. Hindu priests performed rituals at the inauguration of the new parliament building with the prime minister leading the ceremonies in his official capacity. This is a clear departure from the secular moorings of the Indian Constitution.
The government also stresses Hindu civilizational heritage alone. India’s inclusive heritage is ignored. Scholars have argued that post 2014, the BJP regime is fundamentally reinventing the Indian republic from a pluralist, multi-ethnic, multi-religious community to one marked by religious majoritarianism.

articles.title: Vietnam’s Top Leader Concludes Australia Visit With Trade, Defense in Focus
articles.full_text:
In their updated Joint Vision Statement, Canberra and Hanoi identify a more challenging regional security environment.
Vietnamese President To Lam’s visit to Australia this week highlighted the burgeoning relationship between the two countries. Given that much of Australia’s large Vietnamese diaspora remains suspicious of the Communist Party of Vietnam – and South Vietnam flags are often seen flying in suburbs with a concentration of Vietnamese Australians – there is a domestic balancing act that the Australian government needs to perform. However, the convergence of interests between the two countries is now proving the stronger pull.
The focus of Lam’s visit was on new economic and security agreements. The now dominant lens of Australia’s foreign policy perceives economic security as a central pillar of national security.
The economic angle is where the most movement is already happening. Since 2020, two-way trade has doubled, with Vietnam now approaching Australia’s list of top ten trading partners. The specific measures announced this week were mostly incremental: greater agricultural access (including kangaroo meat), and creating smoother services within e-commerce and banking sectors. The low-cost airline Vietjet confirmed it will fly into the new Western Sydney Airport, due to be opened later this year. These are not transformative arrangements, but things that push the relationship forward in important ways. 
The major development was Vietnam approving a license for the Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology (RMIT) to open a campus in Hanoi. The university had already established a campus in Ho Chi Minh City in 2000, and has been keen to establish itself as a major driver of the bilateral relationship, including through the creation of the Australia Vietnam Policy Institute to facilitate building the relationship between the two countries. This is part of a broader push by the Australian university sector to embed itself in Southeast Asia, with four other universities operating in Malaysia and Indonesia. 
Although starting from a low base, the two countries’ security relationship has begun to deepen. This is being driven primarily by shared concerns about China’s activity in the South China Sea. Within their updated Joint Vision Statement, Canberra and Hanoi identify a more challenging regional security environment, marked by strategic competition and military build-up in the Indo-Pacific, and express a shared commitment to a rules-based regional order. Although not mentioning China directly, the statement emphasizes a respect for sovereignty and international law, and the importance of peace and stability in the South China Sea, including freedom of navigation and overflight and adherence to UNCLOS.
To facilitate this vision, the countries have been institutionalizing dialogues through regular meetings between defense and foreign ministers. Yet there is now an attempt to create more practical and substantive cooperation through maritime security, defense intelligence and information sharing, cybersecurity, humanitarian assistance and disaster relief, counterterrorism, military medicine, and the defense industry. The two countries also intend to increase bilateral military education and training as well as multilateral exercises, and seek out paths to greater interoperability. 
A key element to this is filtering cooperation through regional cooperation. The phrase “ASEAN centrality” has become something of a shibboleth repeated by the Australian government when seeking to enhance relations with Southeast Asian countries. It may have less than solid practical implications, but it is how the region wants to frames its diplomacy and engagement, and so it is necessary for Canberra to respect that. 
Due to this, the Joint Vision Statement declared that Australia and Vietnam will work more closely through ASEAN-led mechanisms, particularly the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting-Plus – the annual platform established in 2010 that enables the 11 ASEAN member states to engage with external dialogue partners for regional defense cooperation. Such dialogues are important confidence building mechanisms for Australia and Southeast Asia. 
Australia’s approach to Southeast Asia is based on the idea that no single tool is enough to protect and advance its interests. This means that greater agricultural access, digital economy agreements, and a new university campus in Vietnam are all complementary to securing greater defense cooperation. Each creates a web of intersecting ties that can prove resistant to any potential shocks or attempts at coercion. 
In Vietnam, Australia has a receptive partner as its own diplomatic approach has a similar logic –  diversify economic and security ties across as many partners as possible so that no single relationship, and no single power, gains leverage over Vietnamese decision-making. While some in the Vietnamese diaspora may be displeased with the To Lam’s visit, the foreign policy objectives of Australia will overwhelm their protests.

articles.title: Vietnam, Rare Earths, and the Evolving China Plus One Strategy
articles.full_text:
Vietnam has benefited greatly from foreign firms’ desire to de-risk from China. Can it free itself of dependence on the country’s critical rare earth inputs?
Over the past few years, China Plus One has reshaped global production, helping Vietnam emerge as an important manufacturing base. China Plus One involves companies reducing their excessive dependence on a single production base (i.e., China) by adding capacity elsewhere, which many have already done. However, the next stage of this strategy is likely to be more complicated. Export controls and economic security concerns are exposing vulnerabilities further upstream, particularly in industries that depend on critical minerals. This has demonstrated that even if a company can diversify where it manufactures, it may remain dependent on concentrated supplies of the materials, components, and processing capabilities necessary for that production.
Vietnam illustrates this challenge particularly well. China Plus One has brought major investments and increasingly sophisticated manufacturing activities to the country. Amkor Technology, for example, has invested $1.6 billion in a semiconductor assembly, testing, and packaging facility in Bac Ninh province outside Hanoi. Such investments have deepened Vietnam’s links to technologically intensive global supply chains and have made the security of critical inputs increasingly relevant to the country’s economy.
Among the most important of these inputs are rare earth elements. China remains dominant across the rare-earth value chain, accounting for more than 90 percent of global refined output and permanent-magnet production, according to the International Energy Agency. A product assembled in Vietnam may still depend on rare-earth materials, magnets, or other critical inputs processed in China.

Vietnam is an interesting example, given its own abundant rare earth deposits. While Vietnam is not unique in having significant rare-earth resources – Australia, Brazil and Canada, among others, are also developing alternative rare-earth supply chains – what makes it potentially notable is the combination of these resources with an established low-cost export-oriented manufacturing base. In recent years, the country has developed electronics, automotive and other industries that use components and materials linked to rare-earth supply chains. If Vietnam is able to improve its processing and refining capacity, it could potentially connect its upstream resources with manufacturing activities already integrated into global production networks.
That potential should not be overstated, however. Vietnam’s rare-earth industry remains in its infancy; the country has limited refining capacity, and existing facilities remain concentrated in relatively basic stages of processing. Vietnam Rare Earths operates the country’s only light rare-earth refining facility in Ha Nam province, with an annual capacity of just 5,000 tonnes. Vietnam still lacks the scale of separation and downstream capabilities required for a fully integrated supply chain.
The value of these materials depends on the ability to mine, separate, refine and transform them into inputs for advanced manufacturing. Vietnam’s policy is beginning to address this gap. An amendment to the Law on Geology and Minerals passed in December 2025 classifies rare earths as a “special strategic” mineral and places their exploration, mining, and processing under tighter state control. It also prohibits the export of raw rare-earth materials and places greater emphasis on domestic processing and higher-value products.

In 2010, the two countries agreed to cooperate on rare-earth exploration, mining and processing, including technology transfer and human-resource development, following the vulnerabilities exposed by the 2010 China-Japan rare-earth dispute. More recently, during Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s visit to Vietnam in May, rare-earth development and supply-chain cooperation were again highlighted as strategically important to Japan’s economic security.
Recent corporate investment shows how Vietnam’s manufacturing and critical-mineral stories are beginning to intersect. Its supporting-industry development program for 2026–2035 seeks to strengthen domestic production, increase localization, and deepen the participation of Vietnamese enterprises in global supply chains. The government aims to raise average localization rates in key industries to 40–45 percent by 2030.

China’s dominance in rare earths has been built through decades of investment in processing technologies, industrial infrastructure, downstream manufacturing, and integrated supply chains. articles.title: Myanmar’s Resistance Finally Has a Unified Front
articles.full_text:
The new Steering Council for the Emergence of a Federal Democratic Union could change the course of the country’s conflict.
Civil defense trainees attend a graduation ceremony for a capacity building program run by the Defense Ministry of Myanmar’s National Unity Government in Sagaing Region, Myanmar, Apr. 19, 2026.
I was serving as Dean of the University of Medicine in Yangon when Myanmar’s military staged its coup in February 2021. Overnight, I became an activist in the resistance movement, serving in a variety of roles. Like millions of my fellow citizens, I joined peaceful protests and helped lead the Civil Disobedience Movement.
My involvement soon made me a wanted man, forcing me to flee to a neighboring country before I eventually received refuge in Europe. I was later appointed minister of health and education in the National Unity Government (NUG), which was formed in April 2021 to lead the resistance to the coup.
Since then, throughout what has become known as the Myanmar Spring Revolution, I have witnessed both its triumphs and its setbacks firsthand. Living abroad also allowed me to engage extensively with foreign governments and Myanmar diaspora communities before I returned to Myanmar in 2025. I am now based in one of Myanmar’s liberated areas – territories under the control of revolutionary forces.
Against this backdrop, I believe the recent creation of the Steering Council for the Emergence of a Federal Democratic Union (SCEF) represents the most significant turning point in Myanmar’s resistance movement since the 2021 coup.
Some have dismissed the SCEF as merely another acronym. Nothing could be further from the truth. It represents one of the most consequential political and military realignments in Myanmar’s modern history. It addresses one of the central weaknesses that has long undermined Myanmar’s democratic struggle: the inability of anti-military forces to sustain a unified political and military front across ethnic and ideological lines.
The Steering Council brings together several of Myanmar’s most powerful and politically significant resistance actors, including the Kachin Independence Organization (KIO), the Karen National Union (KNU), the Chin National Front (CNF), the Karenni, the Committee Representing Pyidaungsu Hluttaw (CRPH), the exile parliamentary body, and the NUG. Such broad participation is unprecedented.
For decades, Myanmar’s ethnic resistance organizations (EROs) understood that none could defeat the military on their own. Yet repeated attempts to build durable alliances collapsed under the weight of mistrust, competing interests, ethnic divisions, and external pressures. At the same time, many EROs came to recognize that their remarkable battlefield successes since 2021 would not have been possible without the nationwide Spring Revolution, which fundamentally transformed Myanmar’s political landscape.
One major attempt at unity followed the 1988 uprising with the creation of the Democratic Alliance of Burma, which brought together the KNU, the KIO, the All Burma Students’ Democratic Front, and several other organizations around a shared federal vision. The alliance fractured in 1994 after the KIO signed a ceasefire agreement with the junta. Subsequent ERO coalitions were more limited in scope, focusing primarily on military coordination and territorial defense rather than the development of an inclusive federal political framework that incorporated the Bamar-majority democratic movement.
The Steering Council is different from previous alliances because it integrates political leadership with military coordination. It unites long-established ethnic armed organizations with the post-coup democratic resistance led by the NUG and the CRPH. In doing so, it also addresses the question that I have been repeatedly asked during meetings with foreign officials: whether Myanmar’s anti-junta movement can evolve into a coherent national alternative rather than remain a loose collection of armed groups pursuing divergent political objectives. Some feared that the collapse of military rule might produce fragmentation resembling the post-conflict experiences of Libya or Syria. The emergence of the Steering Council should go a long way toward alleviating those concerns.
The formation of the SCEF has been several years in the making. Discussions began during confidential meetings in Europe in October 2022 and continued through a series of negotiations inside Myanmar and across neighboring countries. This slow and deliberate process reflected the difficulty of building trust among organizations with different political cultures, military structures, and historical grievances.
As an initial step, on January 31, 2024, the CNF, KNU, Karenni, and NUG issued the Joint Position Statement Towards the Annihilation of Military Dictatorship and the Establishment of a Federal Democratic Union. Informally known as the K2C–NUG Position Statement, the document outlined six political objectives that closely resemble those of the Steering Council. The KIO’s formal participation in the Steering Council represents a major breakthrough in coalition-building and provides a roadmap for the eventual inclusion of additional ethnic organizations.
Discussions are also underway with several other EROs. While understandings and frameworks for future collaboration are being developed, the sensitive nature of these negotiations prevents any further public disclosure at this stage.
The Steering Council is the product of years of patient negotiations and incremental consensus-building, making it more likely to endure than previous alliances. Its institutional design also reflects a level of organizational maturity that earlier coalitions lacked. The SCEF has been deliberately structured as a long-term institution capable of leading both wartime resistance and the subsequent political transition.
At the SCEF’s apex is a Strategic Leadership Committee composed of seven senior representatives, one from each member organization. Beneath it operates a Secretariat consisting of 12 senior officials empowered to make operational decisions without constant referral to their respective organizations. This is a deliberate effort to streamline coordination within a movement often criticized for fragmentation and slow decision-making. I serve as one of those 12 Secretariat members.
Supporting the Secretariat are committees responsible for foreign affairs, finance, federal affairs, security, and interior affairs. Resources and funding are intended to be shared equitably, while the Steering Council seeks to present itself internationally as a unified body speaking with one voice.
Alongside the Secretariat is the Military Affairs Coordinating Body, composed of ten senior commanders from member organizations responsible for military operations, procurement, and logistics. It reports directly to the Strategic Leadership Committee.
In effect, the Steering Council institutionalizes what Myanmar’s resistance has historically lacked: unified political leadership directly linked to coordinated military operations. For the first time since the 2021 coup, Myanmar’s principal democratic and ethnic resistance organizations have created a genuinely integrated political and military framework with national ambitions.
Myanmar’s resistance landscape remains extraordinarily complex, and powerful external actors could still complicate efforts to expand or consolidate the coalition. The alliance’s members are fully aware of these challenges, and we understand that our credibility will ultimately depend on demonstrating effective battlefield coordination, measurable progress, and coherent diplomacy abroad.
Several Steering Council representatives have already visited foreign capitals to brief governments, with additional visits planned. Most recently, a briefing was held in Thailand for diplomats and representatives of selected civil society organizations. We have been encouraged by the positive response and optimism expressed by many participants.
The Military’s New Government Will Not Bring Peace
In April, following a widely discredited sham election in December and January, the junta has attempted to rebrand itself as a civilian government. The new president is none other than the former junta chief, while the ruling party remains dominated by former military officers and junta loyalists. This arrangement cannot bring genuine peace or stability because it runs contrary to the people’s aspirations for freedom, democracy, and equality among all ethnic communities.
The major EROs controlling large portions of the country are currently members of the Steering Council and have rejected the new government. The Arakan Army, which controls significant territory in western Myanmar, continues to wage major offensives against the military. Several other EROs governing extensive areas in northeastern Myanmar are not currently engaged in active fighting, despite their remarkable success during the Operation 1027 offensive in late 2023 and 2024, largely because of external pressure.
The claim that the new government, which controls only a handful of major urban centers, can bring peace and stability therefore does not withstand scrutiny. Myanmar is no longer governed exclusively from Naypyidaw. Across large parts of the country, ethnic resistance organizations already provide governance, including local administration, education, healthcare, and other public services.
The Steering Council is the clearest indication yet that Myanmar’s resistance is evolving from a reactive anti-coup movement into an increasingly organized national coalition capable of shaping a post-junta federal order.
In many respects, the Steering Council is laying the institutional foundations for the future state of Myanmar – a process that has repeatedly been interrupted repeatedly by military coups, fragile ceasefires, sham civilian governments, and periods of incomplete democratic rule since the country gained independence in 1948.
The Steering Council offers the people of Myanmar their best opportunity in decades to end military rule and replace perpetual conflict with a new political system capable of delivering lasting peace, security, freedom, democracy, and equality.
For the international community, it presents a rare opportunity to engage with a resistance movement that is increasingly coordinated, politically coherent, and committed to building a democratic federal union capable of bringing long-term stability and prosperity to Myanmar and the wider region.
I was serving as Dean of the University of Medicine in Yangon when Myanmar’s military staged its coup in February 2021. Overnight, I became an activist in the resistance movement, serving in a variety of roles. Like millions of my fellow citizens, I joined peaceful protests and helped lead the Civil Disobedience Movement.
articles.summary: The new Steering Council for the Emergence of a Federal Democratic Union could change the course of the country's conflict.

articles.title: Japan’s Underground Lab Wants to Solve the World’s Nuclear Waste Problem
articles.full_text:
A rare visit to the Horonobe Underground Research Laboratory, where Japanese researchers are testing options for storing radioactive waste.
Scientists visiting the Horonobe Underground Research Laboratory in Hokkaido, Japan.
Reindeer pastures and dairy farms stretch across the flat, windswept plain of Japan’s northernmost prefecture, giving little hint of what lies roughly 300 meters below. Inside the Horonobe Underground Research Laboratory, teams of engineers are trying to answer a question no country has fully solved: how to keep highly radioactive waste isolated from the environment for periods measured not in decades, but in tens of thousands of years.
In May, I gained special access to the facility through the Japan Atomic Energy Agency (JAEA), touring the underground galleries and observing several of the experiments currently underway.
Horonobe is one of only two underground research laboratories Japan has built to study geological disposal of high-level radioactive waste, and the only one still operating. Its counterpart, the Mizunami Underground Research Laboratory in Gifu Prefecture, was built in crystalline rock and was decommissioned in 2022 after its land lease expired. Horonobe, by contrast, sits in Neogene-era sedimentary rock, giving the JAEA a very different and, officials argue, complementary geological environment to study.
The project traces back to November 2000, when the governor of Hokkaido, the mayor of Horonobe town, and the president of the JAEA signed an agreement to permit research on the deep geological environment at the site. Construction and excavation followed over the next two decades, and the laboratory now includes shafts and galleries used to test how engineered barriers, groundwater, and surrounding rock interact over time – the same combination of natural and artificial safeguards that would, in theory, protect a real repository.
Two of the central experiments underway involve what the JAEA calls the “full-scale engineered barrier system performance experiment” and a “solute transport experiment,” both designed to test, at real scale, how bentonite buffers, canisters, and cement-based materials behave once water and pressure are introduced over years rather than months. The JAEA has also been testing how the surrounding sedimentary rock buffers natural disturbances, earthquakes, and groundwater shifts that could compromise a repository’s isolation over the long term.
The JAEA is emphatic on one point, repeated in nearly every briefing given to visitors: Horonobe is a research facility, not a candidate site for Japan’s eventual high-level waste repository. Japanese law formally separates the two functions, and the agency overseeing the actual site-selection process, the Nuclear Waste Management Organization of Japan, operates independently of the JAEA’s research program.
That legal separation has not entirely dissolved local unease. Horonobe is a farming town of roughly 2,000 residents, many of whom have lived for two decades with an underground laboratory in their backyard and, despite official assurances, the lingering question of what happens to the facility once the research concludes.
Japan’s broader search for a permanent repository has proven difficult everywhere it has been raised. Only two municipalities, Suttsu and Kamoenai in Hokkaido, have so far agreed even to preliminary literature-based surveys, and neither has committed to hosting a final site.
What distinguishes Horonobe today is its growing international role. In February 2023, the JAEA and the OECD’s Nuclear Energy Agency (NEA) launched the Horonobe International Project, bringing foreign research organizations into the underground laboratory to work on shared technical problems. The first phase ran through March 2025 with 11 participating organizations from countries including Australia, Bulgaria, Germany, South Korea, Romania, Taiwan, and the United Kingdom, alongside Japan. 
A second phase, running from April 2025 through March 2029, has continued with roughly 10 member organizations pursuing three joint technical tasks: modeling how dissolved substances move through fractured sedimentary rock, integrating different repository design options, and dismantling a full-scale engineered barrier system to see how it performed after years underground.
For countries such as Australia and South Korea – both still in the early stages of building their own waste-management institutions – Horonobe offers something they cannot yet replicate at home: a working underground facility where design assumptions can be tested in real-world conditions. South Korea’s state nuclear research institute has said it is benchmarking its own disposal-performance models against Horonobe data as it prepares to build an underground laboratory of its own in Taebaek. 
NEA officials have described the site as an important international platform for developing and demonstrating repository technology, with plans to eventually extend the laboratory to 500 meters below sea level.
It is difficult to walk through Horonobe without thinking of Onkalo, the repository under construction on the island of Olkiluoto in western Finland, which is set to become the world’s first operational deep geological disposal site for spent nuclear fuel. Having visited Onkalo myself, the contrast with Horonobe is immediately clear. Onkalo is being excavated roughly 400 meters into Precambrian granite bedrock nearly 1.9 billion years old – rock that geologists consider to have remained structurally stable through repeated glacial cycles. Horonobe, by design, tests young, still-consolidating Neogene sedimentary rock, chosen precisely because it represents a geological setting Japan cannot avoid when it eventually has to site a real repository. Much of the country lacks Finland’s kind of ancient crystalline bedrock.
The difference between the two sides is as much political as geological. Posiva Oy, the utility consortium that owns and operates Onkalo, spent roughly two decades developing its technical solution and benefited from a Finnish system in which nuclear waste responsibility stays under public oversight even where the industry itself is privately run, with the national regulator STUK maintaining permanent inspectors on site. That framework was paired with sustained public consultation and a compensation system for the host municipality, Eurajoki, that turned three decades of engagement into local acceptance rather than opposition. Waste is due to begin arriving at Onkalo in 2026, sealed in copper-and-bentonite canisters designed to maintain their integrity for roughly 100,000 years.
Japan, by contrast, has yet to find a single municipality willing to host a final repository, and Horonobe’s own officials go out of their way to stress that the laboratory is not a step toward designating the town as one. 
Finland’s example has not gone unnoticed in Tokyo: Japanese institutions are already among the countries cooperating with Posiva on adapting Finnish containment technology to different geological and regulatory contexts, a channel that runs alongside, but separately from, the JAEA’s own international partnerships through the Horonobe International Project.
That gap helps explain why Horonobe matters beyond Japan’s borders. It is not a repository and, officially, will never become one. But it is one of a small number of places on Earth where engineers can watch, in real time and at full scale, whether the technology underpinning every country’s nuclear waste strategy actually behaves the way computer models predict over years of exposure to rock, water, and pressure.

articles.title: Data of 15 Million Kazakhstanis Allegedly Leaked
articles.full_text:
A hacker claims to have stolen the data from Kazakhstan eGov service. The authorities are investigating the claim.
Hackers have allegedly posted the personal data of 15 million Kazakhstani citizens for sale on the dark web. If confirmed, this would mark the second major breach of Kazakhstani citizen data in a little over a year.
According to RFE/RL, the Mash Telegram channel, which the outlet characterized as linked to the Russian security forces, reported that hackers had put the personal data of 15 million Kazakhstani citizens up for sale on the dark web. The seller reportedly claimed to have obtained the data after hacking Kazakhstan’s eGov service. The file is apparently valued at around $32,000 and, the seller claims, contains passport information, phone numbers, email addresses, document scans, and website passwords.
Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development acknowledged the reports and is reviewing them. In a statement posted to Telegram, the ministry said, “At this time, there is no confirmed evidence of a breach of e-government information systems or that the database in question was obtained directly from eGov.” The ministry cited inconsistencies between the claim and the structure of the eGov platform.
Data breaches are a fact of modern life the world over. Governments, including Kazakhstan’s, have increasingly pushed to digitalize services. On the one hand, the elimination of physical paperwork and office visits speeds service delivery, eliminating layers of bureaucracy and opportunities for petty corruption. But on the other hand, e-government introduces new risks, can obscure decisionmaking, and provides novel opportunities for corruption and crime. 
This latest report of leaked citizen data is not the first breach. In June 2025, the SecuriXy.kz Telegram channel reported that an archive containing information on 16.3 million Kazakhstani citizens had been leaked. The files reportedly contained 15.8 million IINs (individual identification numbers), 17 million phone numbers, alongside full names, dates of birth, and addresses.
At the time, SecuriXy.kz reported, “Analysis shows that most of the records are dated 2022, but relevant data from 2023–2024 was also discovered in the archive. This means the leak is recent and poses a real threat. This data could be used for phishing, document forgery, attacks on eGov and mobile banking accounts, and phone fraud.”
