articles.title: ‘Golden Kamuy’ and Modern Russo-Japanese Relations
articles.full_text:
The manga-turned-anime serves as an important pop cultural piece in understanding Japan’s place in the world, most specifically its historic role with Russia and their Northeast Asian borderlands.
First tankōbon volume cover, featuring Saichi Sugimoto.
Spoiler Alert: Key plot points in “Golden Kamuy” discussed in detail below.
Modern-day relations between Japan and Russia are complex, with one of the most pivotal turning points in the relationship being the 1904-1905 Russo-Japanese War. While the conflict has been extensively studied in academic literature, a popular manga and anime known as “Golden Kamuy” uses the backdrop of the Russo-Japanese War to reevaluate Russo-Japanese relations more broadly, as well as the status of the Ainu and other indigenous Far Eastern people.
“Golden Kamuy,” created by Noda Satoru, ran as a serialized manga from 2014 to 2022. It then spawned a five-season anime series, with its final segment expected to wrap up in late 2026, and several live-action movies. “Golden Kamuy” focuses on Sugimoto Saichi, a veteran of the Russo-Japanese War, and an Ainu girl named Asirpa. The two team up in search of a hidden treasure trove of gold, but they have to piece together a map tattooed across the backs of 24 prisoners who escaped from Abashiri prison. The duo encounters both allies and enemies in their quest.
Location plays a leading role in “Golden Kamuy”: most of the action takes place in Hokkaido, today the northernmost island of Japan and historically the homeland of the Ainu people. A prominent subplot also brings the main characters to Sakhalin, a Russo-Japanese borderland that is today Russian territory; the area has also long been settled by indigenous Ainu, Nivkh, and Uilta/Orok peoples. The interplay of Japanese, Russian, and Ainu cultures in the show, especially as territorial claims changed hands (most notably in the case of Sakhalin), drives the plot forward and showcases how those interactions continue to shape relations in this part of the world today.
In addition, “Golden Kamuy” inserts itself into pivotal moments of Russian and Japanese history by weaving its narrative into real-life historical events. For example, Wilk, the father of Asirpa, became a revolutionary in his youth after suffering under Russian and Japanese colonial encroachment in his homeland of Karafuto (today’s Southern Sakhalin). He dreamed of establishing a Far Eastern federation in Hokkaido and Sakhalin, governed by the Ainu and other Far Eastern indigenous people, to preserve their linguistic and cultural heritage. To achieve this goal, he joined the People’s Will, a Russian anti-monarchist organization, and assassinated Tsar Alexander II by throwing a bag of bombs into his carriage.
Despite the creative liberties Noda took by reimagining Wilk as the assassin of the tsar, other elements of this plot point reflect historical fact: the People’s Will was an actual revolutionary movement most famous for carrying out a bomb attack against Tsar Alexander II in March 1881, prematurely ending his reign and reversing Russia’s progressive path with the authoritarian turns of his successors Tsar Alexander III and Tsar Nicholas II.
“Golden Kamuy” also touches upon the Meiji Restoration: Hijikata Toshizou, one of the main ensemble characters, is an elderly samurai based on a real-life historical figure of the same name. Meanwhile, his fictional counterpart in “Golden Kamuy” was imprisoned at Abashiri prison; after he escaped, he still strived to reestablish the Republic of Ezo with the hidden gold.

The loss of the war is arguably one of the catalysts for the 1905 Revolution and ultimately paved the way for the Bolsheviks to seize power in 1917. Kuropatkin and the collection Русско-японская война 1904–1905 гг. в воспоминаниях.)

Discrimination and pressure to assimilate into Japanese society virtually erased numerous aspects of Ainu cultural identity, including the now critically endangered Ainu language. That being said, recent years have signaled a renaissance of renewed pride in Ainu identity. Language revitalization programs, including immersive classes and AI speech synthesis, are helping to combat Ainu linguistic extinction. The Upopoy National Ainu Museum and Park, opened in 2020, serves as an integral center for preserving Ainu history and culture.
“Golden Kamuy” itself has proven instrumental in sparking modern interest in the Ainu by being featured in international artistic and cultural exhibitions and boosting tourism to Hokkaido. Thus, while the Ainu have faced enormous struggles over the past decades, if not centuries, efforts such as “Golden Kamuy” fight to ensure that this culture’s legacy will endure in the future by educating a new generation of manga and anime-loving Japanese (and global fans) about the existence and importance of the Ainu.
The interconnection between pop culture and geopolitics is arguably one of the lesser-known sub-genres of international relations, but there is growing interest in understanding it. As for Russo-Japanese relations today, they are currently at a historic low due to the long-contested Southern Kuril Islands (which Russia calls the Northern Territories) territorial dispute and Japanese support for Ukraine during the seemingly never-ending Russo-Ukrainian War. It then spawned a five-season anime series, with its final segment expected to wrap up in late 2026, and several live-action movies. “Golden Kamuy” focuses on Sugimoto Saichi, a veteran of the Russo-Japanese War, and an Ainu girl named Asirpa. The two team up in search of a hidden treasure trove of gold, but they have to piece together a map tattooed across the backs of 24 prisoners who escaped from Abashiri prison. The duo encounters both allies and enemies in their quest.

articles.title: The Mecca Pact and America’s Reduced Leverage in West Asia
articles.full_text:
Erosion of U.S. influence could, in the long run, impact arms sales, the negotiation of military basing rights, and the management of regional crises.
The signing of the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Türkiye on August 7 is a significant development. The pact is the first formal regional security agreement to be formed as a direct result of the conflict between the U.S. and Iran. The agreement reflects the lessons that key regional actors have drawn from the crisis as they seek to redefine their place within a security order long dominated by the U.S.
The West Asia war has revealed that the American defense umbrella in the form of forward bases in the region is not adequate in protecting Saudi Arabia and the other Gulf Arab states from Iranian attacks. Rather, the U.S. military presence in these states pulled them directly into the conflict, making them targets of Iran and its regional allies. Additionally, the Israeli military’s approach to the Palestinian question and its bombing of the people of Gaza have drawn widespread ire in the Muslim world.
For decades, Washington served as the sole security guarantor in the Gulf. The emergence of a formal defense pact among key regional players that excludes the U.S. is may chip away at Washington’s leverage in the region. While this erosion of influence may not become fully apparent in the short term, it is likely to assume greater significance in the coming years, particularly with respect to arms sales, the negotiation of military basing rights, and the management of regional crises.
One may argue that as a result of the pact the U.S. will now be indirectly constrained by decisions taken jointly by Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan. For instance, the Mecca Pact stipulates that an attack on one country will be regarded as an attack upon all. While the signatories have not publicly elaborated the precise circumstances under which the idea of collective commitment would be activated, it is reasonable to conclude that they have reached internal understandings regarding the scenarios that would trigger such a response.
It does seem that Washington sees little issue with the Mecca Agreement. American officials have refrained from opposing the agreement, with analysts noting that it aligns with Washington’s interests for regional burden-sharing. In practice, however, the U.S. holds no formal obligations under the pact. However, its deep military ties with Saudi Arabia, Turkiye, and Pakistan mean Washington cannot easily disentangle itself should a crisis erupt amid ambiguity surrounding the pact’s scope.
It is important to note that this pact has taken shape among countries bound by deep historical, religious and defense ties, whose interests have converged amid the shifting geopolitical landscape of West Asia during the Iran-U.S. war. Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye have long maintained strong military cooperation. Last year, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan concluded a bilateral Strategic Mutual Defense Agreement. Similarly, Türkiye and Pakistan have been collaborating on naval projects, fighter jet development and joint exercises.
Furthermore, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye have established strong defense ties in recent years. A major turning point in this regard occurred in 2023 when Saudi Arabia signed a massive defense contract to acquire Bayraktar Akinci unmanned combat aerial vehicles (UCAVs) from Türkiye’s Baykar. The deal included agreements between Saudi Military Industries and Baykar for technology transfer, local assembly, testing and joint production inside the Kingdom. In a way, this directly aligned with Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030 objective to localize more than 50 percent of its military spending. This existing Saudi, Turkish, and Pakistani defense industry collaboration made it only natural to form a defensive alliance that is expected to foster deeper military integration in the years ahead.
Arguably, Washington has been compelled to accept the arrangement due to the transformation of regional realities where it cannot fully ensure conflict resolution. The agreement could not realistically have materialized prior to the Iran–U.S. conflict that started last year. Still, from the American perspective, there is relative advantage in permitting a pact among three states that already possess established linkages with the U.S., rather than allowing unpredictable security vacuums to be filled by non-aligned actors such as Iran.
This does not, however, suggest that the pact is directed against Iran.
Early diplomatic exchanges suggest that Iran has, if anything, been kept informed about this arrangement. A particularly symbolic illustration in this regard is the telephone conversation between Pakistan’s Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar and his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi following the signing of the Mecca Pact.
According to the Pakistani Foreign Office statement, Dar “shared the contours of the recently signed Makkah Joint Defense Agreement between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye, underscoring its objectives of strengthening strategic cooperation and contributing to regional peace and security.” On his part, Araghchi expressed appreciation for the briefing. In the same exchange, the Iranian foreign minister conveyed the latest status of bilateral talks with Oman concerning a suitable route for the safe passage of ships through the Strait of Hormuz.
Separately, the spokesman for Iran’s Foreign Ministry characterized the Mecca Agreement as a “sign of a changing perception among regional states,” observing that the signatories have come to recognize that security cannot be secured through reliance on foreign powers. Iran has seemingly welcomed the agreement both as validation of its own long-standing view of regional security and as a potential foundation for a broader collective security framework.
Iran’s foreign ministry spokesman emphasized that “regional security is indivisible.” Any initiative that correctly identifies the principal threat could contribute to the strengthening of security across West Asia, he said. In this reading, Tehran appears to regard the Mecca agreement as arguably correctly identifying, or something closer to the Iranian view regarding the prevailing threat environment and as trying to establish a longer-term structure to address it.
If the telephone exchange between the Pakistani and Iranian foreign ministers and the Iranian Foreign Ministry’s statement are indicative, they point toward an emerging regional security and diplomatic architecture in West Asia, the outlines of which have been sketched by the Mecca Agreement and within which Iran is likely to play a future role.
Significantly, Saudi Arabia has already moved to address contentious questions surrounding the pact. The Saudi Gazette quoted Saudi Deputy Minister for Public Diplomacy, Amb. Dr. Rayed Krimly, who clarified that the agreement “is not intended to establish a military axis or sectarian bloc and is not linked to nuclear ambitions or an arms race.”
Krimly further emphasized that the accord “does not threaten the security of any country in the region and should not be viewed as an escalation of tensions between any two states.”
In a nutshell, the Mecca agreement suggests that Pakistan’s diplomatic role in bridging divides and facilitating communication across the Persian Gulf will expand under this new framework. Moreover, the three signatories are expected to assume greater responsibility for resolving differences among themselves through diplomatic means. Over time, the framework may evolve to encompass additional regional participants, including Iran, other Gulf states and elsewhere.
It remains to be seen under what precise circumstances the agreement might be formally invoked.
Nevertheless, the Mecca Pact represents a significant structural shift in which regional countries such as Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Türkiye are seeking to increase their strategic autonomy. This, in the long run, could help diminish the monopoly the Americans long exercised over West Asia’s regional security dynamics and their core interests.

articles.title: Why the Pacific Islands Forum Should Watch Taiwan’s East Coast
articles.full_text:
The waters east of Taiwan sit within a strategically integrated maritime space stretching from Northeast Asia, through Micronesia and Melanesia, to Polynesia.
Chair and Solomon Islands Minister for Foreign Affairs and External Trade, Hon. Rick Houenipwela, joined Secretary General, Baron Divavesi Waqa, in taking questions from regional and international media during a press conference following the recent Foreign Ministers Meeting.
Ahead of the 55th Pacific Islands Forum (PIF), scheduled to take place August 30 to September 4 in Palau, Pacific Island leaders failed to reach consensus on a joint statement criticizing China’s submarine-based ballistic missile testing in the Pacific. The split reflects intensifying great-power competition and divergent threat perceptions between external powers and Pacific governments. Yet China’s growing military activities have clearly heightened concerns among forum members. 
Besides missile testing, another less visible source of pressure lies in the growing normalization of Chinese naval and coast guard activity in the waters east of Taiwan, a development the PIF has yet to fully connect to its own maritime interests. This maritime gateway east of Taiwan leads directly into the exclusive economic zones that the forum seeks to protect and deserves greater attention from Pacific Island states. 
Rather than a distant flashpoint, the waters east of Taiwan form the northern hinge of the same maritime arc that runs through Micronesia and Melanesia, linked by overlapping sea lines of communication and interconnected ocean current systems. This deep-water gateway to the Blue Pacific is increasingly being trespassed and pressured by Chinese government vessels.
Beijing appears to be using unresolved maritime boundary negotiations involving Japan and the Philippines as justification for expanding coast guard patrols and deploying more research and survey vessels east of Taiwan. Many of these platforms are converted former naval vessels, underscoring the increasingly blurred line between maritime law enforcement and strategic power projection. By increasing the frequency and persistence of deployments along Taiwan’s Pacific coast, Beijing appears to be seeking to normalize a sustained Chinese maritime security presence in the Blue Pacific waters. 
This expansion is unfolding alongside a broader rise in Chinese naval activity in the Western Pacific. Since 2025, the Liaoning and Shandong carrier strike groups have conducted operations and flight exercises beyond the first island chain. With China’s third aircraft carrier, the Fujian, reaching full operational capability, Beijing is moving closer to sustaining a regular carrier presence in the Western Pacific.
The growing presence of coast guard, research, survey, and naval vessels east of Taiwan suggests that China is gradually extending its maritime operating space from the Taiwan Strait into Taiwan’s Pacific approaches.
For Pacific Island countries, this expanding presence should not be viewed simply as an extension of cross-strait tensions. It could increase uncertainty along commercial shipping routes, raise maritime insurance premiums, lengthen transit times, and complicate the movement of energy, food, and other essential imports through the corridor linking Northeast Asia with Palau, the Federated States of Micronesia, Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands, and the wider Pacific.  
Even without an armed conflict, heightened tensions or more frequent military exercises could generate delays, rerouting, and higher transportation costs for states that are highly dependent on this maritime corridor. China’s expanding naval reach east of Taiwan therefore has implications well beyond Taiwan, intersecting directly with the maritime trade routes and supply chains on which Pacific Island countries depend.
The PIF’s diplomatic motto of being “friends to all and enemies to none” should not be mistaken for strategic insulation, particularly as the maritime status quo east of Taiwan is being reshaped by China’s growing presence and expanding military activity. In a worst-case Taiwan contingency, Beijing could seek to push through the Taiwan–Philippines–Melanesia corridor and constrain U.S. and allied access to the Western Pacific, regardless of whether any PIF member is involved in the conflict. 
For Pacific Island states, preserving free, open, and non-militarized sea lines of communication across the Western Pacific is therefore a vital interest and it should be articulated clearly before shifts in the regional balance of power become more difficult to reverse. The PIF’s “Ocean of Peace” framing should recognize the waters east of Taiwan as part of the same interconnected Pacific maritime space, rather than a separate area.
The Blue Pacific is a Pacific-led regional identity, not a corridor encompassing Taiwan’s east coast, and the argument here is not to redefine that identity. Rather, it is to recognize that the waters east of Taiwan sit within a strategically integrated maritime space stretching from Northeast Asia, through Micronesia and Melanesia, to Polynesia, where developments at one end can directly affect access, connectivity, and security at the other. Recognizing this interdependence is a matter of practical maritime awareness, not a request that Pacific states reframe their own identity or take sides in cross-strait politics.
What is at stake is neither alignment with one great power against another nor a choice between alignment and non-alignment. The more fundamental interest is preserving a maritime space in which all actors can navigate freely and maintain economic and commercial access without coercion, intimidation, or militarization.
Even if PIF members cannot agree on specific issues, such as China’s ballistic missile testing, they should still be able to forge a broader agreement on preserving a free, open, peaceful, and resilient Blue Pacific maritime corridor. That means the Ocean of Peace framework should be able to cover the waters east of Taiwan as a critical component of the broader Blue Pacific maritime domain. The forum could extend information sharing on vessel movements and coast guard activity to this corridor, providing Pacific Island states earlier warning of disruptions to the shipping lanes their economies depend on. 
Such an arrangement could provide a common foundation for the PIF to work with willing Pacific partners on maritime domain awareness, infrastructure resilience, and the security of regional sea lines of communication. Rather than requiring consensus on the behavior of any particular major power, this approach would anchor cooperation in a shared interest in an integrated Pacific maritime space that remains open, accessible, and resilient to coercion and disruption.

Rather than requiring consensus on the behavior of any particular major power, this approach would anchor cooperation in a shared interest in an integrated Pacific maritime space that remains open, accessible, and resilient to coercion and disruption.
articles.summary: The waters east of Taiwan sit within a strategically integrated maritime space stretching from Northeast Asia, through Micronesia and Melanesia, to Polynesia.

articles.title: Symbolic Concessions, No Implementation: Myanmar’s Promises of Rohingya Repatriation
articles.full_text:
Myanmar’s latest pledge to repatriate 300,000 Rohingya refugees cannot be viewed as a credible commitment. It’s yet another iteration of a well-established diplomatic pattern.
Rohingya children gather sticks at a refugee camp in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, March 2018.
On July 29, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim remarked that Myanmar had agreed to repatriate 300,000 Rohingya refugees from Bangladesh and 5,000 from Malaysia. Subsequently, Malaysian and Bangladeshi media outlets enthusiastically disseminated the news. However, the very next day, Bangladeshi State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed stated that Myanmar had forwarded no such proposal to Bangladesh, and while the two sides maintain contact, the topic of the repatriation of 300,000 refugees has not been discussed. 
While people may be tempted to view this event in the context of the domestic politics of Malaysia, it, in fact, confirms a long-standing pattern of behavior on the part of the Myanmar government toward the protracted Rohingya crisis.
In 2017-2018, the Myanmar government orchestrated “cleansing operations” in northern Rakhine State, leading to the exodus of more than 750,000 Rohingyas to neighboring Bangladesh. There they joined some 300,000 Rohingya refugees, who had been residing in Bangladesh since the late 1970s or the 1990s. The exodus of the Rohingyas was accompanied by disturbing reports of war crimes — massacres, sexual assaults, arson, plunder, and others — committed by the Myanmar military, the Tatmadaw, against the Rohingya. The United Nations Human Rights Council (UNHRC) deemed Myanmar’s actions to be “ethnic cleansing,” while the United States recognized it as a “genocide.” Currently, Bangladesh hosts some 1.5 million Rohingya refugees, making it one of the largest hosts of refugees anywhere in the world.
Bangladesh’s own precarious socio-economic conditions preclude the possibility of successful local integration of Rohingya refugees. And no third country is willing to resettle them en masse. Therefore, the only realistic option for the resolution of the protracted refugee crisis is the safe, voluntary, dignified, and sustainable repatriation of the refugees to their homeland. Accordingly, from the very outset, Bangladesh has sought to ensure the return of the refugees to Myanmar. Dhaka has resorted to bilateral, trilateral, and multilateral mechanisms to bring this about, but in each instance, Myanmar has delicately skirted responsibility for the Rohingya.
For instance, on November 23, 2017, Bangladesh and Myanmar concluded a memorandum of understanding (MoU) on the repatriation of Rohingya refugees in Naypyidaw. Myanmar pledged to initiate the process of repatriation within two months, and agreed to take back 300 refugees per day. However, not a single Rohingya refugee was repatriated under the MoU. Nevertheless, Naypyidaw used the MoU to deflect strong international criticism of their actions, portray the crisis as a “bilateral issue” between Myanmar and Bangladesh, and demonstrate their commitment to the resolution of the Rohingya crisis.
Upon the failure of the bilateral MoU, on April 13, 2018, Bangladesh and the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) concluded an MoU on the repatriation of the Rohingya, and the UNHCR and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) signed an MoU with Myanmar on June 6, 2018, in a similar spirit. That MoU was extended for a year in May 2019, and again in May 2020. Through this, Myanmar accepted responsibility for taking back the Rohingya, and demonstrated a lot of activities, such as the verification of tens of thousands of refugees and the opening of transit centers. However, no Rohingya refugees were officially repatriated during this period, as the refugees themselves were apprehensive of repatriation without guarantees of the protection of their rights. Naypyidaw was unwilling to provide such guarantees.
Upon the failures of the U.N.-mediated MoUs, in March 2023, Bangladesh and Myanmar, through Chinese mediation, announced a “pilot program” repatriating small groups of Rohingya refugees to Myanmar. Again, Myanmar demonstrated its commitment to repatriation through the dispatch of officials to Rohingya camps in Cox’s Bazar and the identification of 1,140 Rohingyas for repatriation. However, the process was soon stalled, and the proposed repatriation did not take place. Afterward, the outbreak of war in Rakhine State between the Tatmadaw and the Arakan Army put the issue of Rohingya repatriation on the back-burner.
On April 4, 2025, after negotiations between Bangladesh and Myanmar, the latter expressed its willingness to repatriate 180,000 Rohingya refugees who had been verified by Myanmar between 2018 and 2020. However, by that time, Myanmar had effectively lost control of some 80 percent of Rakhine State, including the Maungdaw District where the majority of the refugees used to live. Hence, Myanmar was in no position to implement its own pledge. In fact, it is possible that Myanmar made this symbolic concession to Dhaka to decrease the latter’s interest in the U.N.-proposed “humanitarian channel” to Rakhine State via its territory. As soon as the interim government of Bangladesh, owing to substantial internal and external pressures, abandoned the proposal, Myanmar demonstrated no further interest in the repatriation of the 180,000 refugees.
After analyzing the behavior of Myanmar since 2017, a distinct pattern emerges. Whenever Myanmar is faced with political or strategic pressure, either from Bangladesh or the international community or local actors, it appears willing to make concessions and repatriate the Rohingya refugees. However, it has consistently reneged on its commitments and displayed that it has no serious intention of taking back the Rohingya. This pattern has been repeated after the bilateral MoU in 2017, the U.N.-mediated MoU in 2018-2021, the Chinese-mediated “pilot program” in 2023, and the bilateral understandings of 2025.
The recent statements about the prospective repatriation of 300,000 refugees from Bangladesh must be viewed through Myanmar’s patterned behavior. Malaysia hosts more than 126,000 Rohingya refugees, and recently, anti-Rohingya sentiments are on the rise among segments of Malaysia’s population. Hence, Malaysia, a member-state of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), is exerting diplomatic pressure on Myanmar for the repatriation of the refugees at least partially on the basis of its own domestic political pressure. Bangladesh has consistently sought the support of ASEAN in general and Malaysia in particular to accelerate the repatriation of the Rohingyas. In response, Naypyidaw has made big promises about the repatriation. However, considering that 90 percent of Rakhine State is under the control of the Arakan Army now, Myanmar is currently in no position to repatriate the Rohingyas to their homeland. Hence, Myanmar’s promises of repatriating 300,000 Rohingyas from Bangladesh is rhetorical at best.
Beyond questions of capacity, Myanmar also currently lacks the political and legal conditions required for safe and sustainable repatriation. Sustainable return of the Rohingyas should be linked to guarantees of citizenship, freedom of movement, physical security, access to livelihoods, and independent international monitoring – conditions that remain absent. The fragmentation of authority in Rakhine State between the military-controlled Union Government and the Arakan Army-controlled Arakan People’s Revolutionary Government (APRG) further complicates the implementation of any repatriation arrangement, regardless of diplomatic declarations. Hence, announcements of large-scale returns function primarily as instruments of political rhetoric for Myanmar rather than concrete commitments. Until these structural impediments are addressed, periodic pledges of repatriation are likely to remain diplomatic narratives instead of executable policy.
Myanmar’s latest pledge to repatriate 300,000 Rohingya refugees should therefore be interpreted not as a credible commitment but as another iteration of a well-established diplomatic pattern. Since 2017, Myanmar has responded to successive bilateral, trilateral, and multilateral initiatives with symbolic concessions without meaningful implementation, enabling Naypyidaw to ease external pressure while avoiding substantive responsibility. Current military realities in the beleaguered Rakhine State, coupled with the absence of legal protections, security guarantees, and unified territorial control, further diminish the feasibility of Myanmar’s proposed large-scale repatriation. Accordingly, durable resolution of the Rohingya crisis depends not on periodic political declarations but on verifiable structural changes within Myanmar and sustained international engagement that ensures any future repatriation is safe, voluntary, dignified, and genuinely sustainable.

articles.title: Reclaiming the Backyard: ASEAN’s Realpolitik Push on Myanmar
articles.full_text:
A Thailand-led push to re-engage the country’s military-backed government is an attempt to prevent the bloc’s diplomatic marginalization.
Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Sihasak Phuangketkeow (right) meets with Than Swe, the foreign minister of Myanmar’s military junta, in Phuket, Thailand, Feb. 18, 2026.
In late 2025, nearly five years after the February 2021 coup, the military junta held a multi-phase election. The polls, which were heavily skewed in favor of the military, produced the expected outcome: the military proxy Union Solidarity and Development Party won 232 of 263 seats in the lower house of the Union Parliament and 109 of 157 seats in the upper house. The election was intended to put a thin veneer of legitimacy on the military dictatorship in order to gain partial re-entry into the international community while continuing its war against the country’s resistance elements. Following the military-administered election, Min Aung Hlaing officially assumed the presidency in April 2026, framing the transition as the constitutional fulfillment of a return to civilian governance.
This domestic political shift inaugurated a carefully orchestrated diplomatic campaign across key neighboring states, which took Min Aung Hlaing to India, Laos, China, and Thailand, designed to launder regime legitimacy, secure critical border trade, and hedge against Western sanctions. Rather than signaling a complete resolution of domestic conflicts, this regional pivot reflects a strategic calibration by neighboring Asian powers that prioritize border stability, maritime security, and economic corridors over concerns about Myanmar’s internal affairs.
From the perspective of the administration in Naypyidaw, the formal transition to a civilian government under the 2008 Constitution provides an exit ramp from pariah status toward institutional normalization. To facilitate this regional re-engagement, the government made a number of strategic, low-cost domestic concessions. Most notably, in late April, it moved Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi from prison to house arrest in an effort to soften regional criticism without surrendering any real executive authority. It then allowed her to meet with a representative of the International Committee for the Red Cross on August 3, offering proof of life.
Concurrently, Min Aung Hlaing has pushed back against ASEAN’s Five-Point Consensus, a plan for resolving the country’s conflict, arguing that the 2021 roadmap requires modification to reflect the operational realities of Myanmar’s newly established civilian administration. Importantly, he hedged his criticism by stating that his administration would “respond to non-constructive actions” by unnamed member states “on a case-by-case basis.”
To consolidate this post-election reality, Naypyidaw initiated a sequenced series of overseas visits across its immediate geographic perimeter. The diplomatic tour began with an official visit to India, where talks between Min Aung Hlaing and senior Indian leaders focused heavily on maritime domain awareness and border stabilization. Building upon existing defense frameworks, New Delhi and Naypyidaw reaffirmed their bilateral agreements regarding White Shipping Information Sharing and coastal surveillance radar systems in the Bay of Bengal, while coordinating counter-insurgency operations along the Mizoram-Chin State border. Min Aung Hlaing subsequently traveled to Laos, securing an initial ASEAN diplomatic beachhead by signing joint feasibility studies for Mekong hydropower development and establishing sister-city relations between Vientiane and Naypyidaw.
Min Aung Hlaing then traveled to Beijing in June for a summit with President Xi Jinping. Beijing accorded the Myanmar leader full state honors, and the two sides signed 18 bilateral Memorandums of Understanding. These agreements included Myanmar’s formal endorsement of China’s Global Security Initiative, Global Development Initiative, and Global Civilization Initiative, while advancing administrative protocols for agricultural trade and the facilitation of cross-border transport across the Greater Mekong Subregion.
However, a nuanced analysis of the summit reveals a deliberate separation between political symbolism and economic risk exposure. While China provided significant diplomatic validation, Beijing conspicuously withheld new financial commitments and construction agreements for flagship China-Myanmar Economic Corridor megaprojects, including the Kyaukphyu Deep-Sea Port and the Muse–Mandalay Railway. During bilateral talks, Xi explicitly conditioned future heavy infrastructure investments on “ensured security,” demanding that Naypyidaw guarantee the safety of Chinese personnel, pipelines, and strategic assets amid ongoing fighting with the Arakan Army in Rakhine State and ethnic armed organizations along the border with China. By granting diplomatic recognition while pausing major capital injections, Beijing effectively deployed a strategy of diplomatic endorsement paired with strict financial hedging.
The next destination on Min Aung Hlaing’s itinerary was Thailand, where he was welcomed with full state honors this week. Thailand’s shift toward “calibrated engagement” with Myanmar under Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul represents a pragmatic response to severe border insecurity. The government in Bangkok faces complex border challenges, including the ongoing territorial conflict along its border with Cambodia alongside the spillover from the civil war in Myanmar, including renewed refugee flows and the presence of transnational scam syndicates along the two nations’ shared border. This point is essential to understanding how pragmatism, rather than idealism, dictates Thai foreign policy. And as a frontline state, Thailand’s voice carries significant weight in ASEAN.
Under Anutin, Thailand has pushed ASEAN to normalize its relationship with Myanmar. It brokered an “informal meeting” between ASEAN’s foreign ministers and Myanmar’s foreign minister on July 12, and hosted Min Aung Hlaing for an official state visit in Bangkok aimed at stabilizing border trade, enhancing intelligence sharing on organized crime, and encouraging Myanmar’s gradual reintegration into regional forums including ASEAN. Bangkok’s re-engagement has been framed by Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuantketkeow’s 3R’s framework, which seeks to simultaneously allow Thailand to diplomatically reemerge from its two-decade hiatus, stabilize Thailand’s frontiers, and elevate ASEAN’s relevance in regional affairs.
Thailand’s “3R” strategy outlines a regional approach for re-engaging Myanmar. (The first “R” stands for regionalism.) It envisions shifting ASEAN’s stance from the fractured Five-Point Consensus toward constructive engagement, similar to the bloc’s pre-2011 diplomatic framework. The second “R,” relevance, attempts to elevate Thailand’s global profile while restoring ASEAN’s authority and centrality in regional affairs. Lastly, the third “R,” resilience, focuses on enhancing regional security against transnational threats, a process that ultimately hinges on Myanmar’s reintegration into ASEAN.
The Thai engagement initiative highlights a broader structural realignment within ASEAN regarding the Myanmar crisis. Thailand has convinced the Philippines, ASEAN’s current chair, and Indonesia, the bloc’s largest member, to engage Naypyidaw. With Cambodia, Laos and Vietnam already on board with engagement and Malaysia shifting, the region is approaching a diplomatic tipping point. Timor-Leste, Malaysia, and Singapore still occupy a principled position of non-recognition but are now in a distinct minority. ASEAN is shifting toward a dual-track strategy: maintaining the Five-Point Consensus as its overarching diplomatic standard while permitting frontline member states to pursue bilateral dialogues and informal multi-stakeholder consultations with both Naypyidaw and ethnic armed organizations.
Recent diplomatic engagements between Myanmar and its neighbors demonstrate that many Asian powers prioritize state capacity, border security, and open trade corridors over the democratic norms that still govern Western policy toward Myanmar. In other words, neighboring states are actively adapting to changing political realities in a bid to safeguard their strategic and economic interests.
Thailand’s push for a calibrated re-engagement with Myanmar, supported by alignment and complementary diplomatic tracks from key maritime actors like the Philippines and Indonesia, represents a calculated attempt to reassert “ASEAN Centrality” against the increased importance of other external Asian powers. Following Min Aung Hlaing’s high-profile bilateral visits to Beijing and New Delhi, ASEAN faced the prospect of becoming a marginalized observer of events in its own backyard. By shifting ASEAN towards a flexible, dual-track framework that pairs formal adherence to the Five-Point Consensus with pragmatic, ground-level dialogue, Thailand and its regional partners are attempting to reinsert ASEAN into the milieu of regional influence. This will not prevent China and India from exercising influence, but perhaps rebalance ASEAN to begin demonstrating economic influence on a Myanmar which is hemorrhaging growth and shifting to an extractive economic footing.
Ultimately, this recalibration demonstrates an intentional effort to restore collective Southeast Asian agency, ensuring that ASEAN – rather than external great powers – retains the institutional influence necessary to dictate security dynamics, mediate conflict, and safeguard its own strategic perimeter.

Ultimately, this recalibration demonstrates an intentional effort to restore collective Southeast Asian agency, ensuring that ASEAN – rather than external great powers – retains the institutional influence necessary to dictate security dynamics, mediate conflict, and safeguard its own strategic perimeter.
articles.summary: A Thailand-led push to re-engage the country's military-backed government is an attempt to prevent the bloc's diplomatic marginalization.

articles.title: Indonesia’s President Nominates Central Bank Deputy as New Governor
articles.full_text:
The rupiah rose slightly on news of Destry Damayanti’s nomination, which will now pass to the House of Representatives for approval.
Buildings in the center of Jakarta, Indonesia.
Indonesia’s President Prabowo Subianto has nominated Destry Damayanti, a long-time central bank deputy, as the next governor of the institution, an official announced yesterday.
State Secretary Prasetyo Hadi confirmed that the nomination was submitted to the House of Representatives through a presidential letter, along with names of nominees for Bank of Indonesia (BI)’s senior deputy role, which Destry previously filled.
Destry Damayanti, a seasoned economist and former chief economist at the state lender Bank Mandiri, has served as the interim governor of BI since the unexpected resignation of Perry Warjiyo last month for “personal reasons.” Perry had served as BI’s governor of the central bank since 2018 and still had three years to run on his term.
Both appointments must be approved by lawmakers, but given the size of Prabowo’s majority in the House, this is likely to be little more than a formality. If (or when) she is approved, Destry, who has also worked for Citibank and served on the board of commissioners for the Indonesia Deposit Insurance Corporation, will become the first woman to take on the role on a permanent basis.
The announcement delivered a small fillip to the rupiah, which closed yesterday at 17,755 to the U.S. dollar, gaining 142 points, or 0.79 percent, from its previous close of 17,897.
The markets’ response hints at the fragile state of investor confidence in Indonesia. Since taking office in October 2024, Prabowo has pursued high-spending populist policies, including a multibillion-dollar free meal program, which have widened the fiscal deficit and pushed it toward its legally mandated ceiling of 3 percent of GDP. The former general has also increased the state’s involvement in the Indonesian economy in a bid to maximize the country’s return from natural resources and international trade.
These policies, along with the firing of respected Finance Minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati last September, have unsettled investors and undermined Indonesia’s hard-won reputation for fiscal conservatism.
In March, both Moody’s and Fitch announced ratings outlook downgrades for the country, with the latter citing the “increasing ⁠policy uncertainty and erosion of Indonesia’s policy mix consistency and credibility” and the “growing centralization of policymaking authority.” This came shortly after the global index provider MSCI threatened to downgrade Indonesia to “frontier market” status due to a number of transparency concerns in its stock market. (It is set to announce its verdict in November.)
At the same time, the rupiah has fallen to record lows this year, passing the psychological threshold of 18,000 rupiah to the U.S. dollar in June.
Coming against this backdrop, Perry’s resignation could not have come at a worse time. While he claimed to have resigned for personal reasons, Reuters reported that it followed a “major disagreement” with Finance Minister Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa over the use of liquidity to support Prabowo’s expansive fiscal agenda.
There were fears that Prabowo might nominate his nephew Thomas Djiwandono, whom he appointed as a deputy governor of BI in February of this year, for the top post at the central bank.

He warned in particular that risk premiums would rise if BI were to prematurely cut rates or provide liquidity to fund Prabowo’s expensive social programs.

articles.title: Art, Surveillance, and the Politics of Memory in Southeast Asia
articles.full_text:
In recent years, the region has seen a worrying rise of moral policing and restrictions on cultural expression.
Anti-junta graffiti seen during anti-coup protests in Mandalay, Myanmar, Feb.9, 2021.
Across Southeast Asia, artists and cultural rights defenders are increasingly being cast as threats – to public morality, political order and dominant narratives about gender, sexuality, identity, and belonging.
This is especially true for queer and trans artists, whose bodies, stories, and performances often challenge the boundaries that states, religious authorities, and conservative movements seek to impose. When they are surveilled or attacked, or their work is censored, the consequences touch the foundations of civic space: the right to speak, gather, remember, imagine, and contest power.
ArtsEquator’s Southeast Asia Artistic Freedom RADAR Database documents this reality across Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Thailand, and Vietnam. In its 2025 report, RADAR recorded 159 challenges to artistic freedom across the seven countries. The findings closely mirror those of the CIVICUS Monitor, which rated Myanmar and Vietnam as “Closed,” Cambodia, Thailand, and the Philippines as “Repressed,” and Malaysia and Indonesia as “Obstructed.”
This matters because attacks on artistic freedom often serve as warnings about the health of civic life. Where artists are censored, surveilled, attacked, or forced into silence, broader patterns of repression are already at work.
While navigating the RADAR database, I came across “moral policing” as a category of violations faced by artists and cultural rights workers. In practice, moral policing punishes artists and communities whose work challenges artificial boundaries around gender, sexuality, faith, tradition, or national identity. It does not always manifest as an outright ban or formal legal charge. More often, it takes shape through public accusations, social pressure, police scrutiny, cancelled performances, restrictions on distribution, withdrawal of support, online harassment, physical attacks, surveillance, or the destruction of artworks.
As I dug deeper, it became evident how often LGBTQ activism and artistic expression appeared in work targeted by this category. This mirrors a trend Urgent Action Fund Asia and Pacific (UAF A&P) has been recording across its learning reports: that queer, trans and LGBTQ communities across Asia and the Pacific are increasingly being targeted through legislation, political and social attacks, isolation, and reduced resources for activism.
This broader pattern of moral policing and restrictions on cultural expression is visible in specific cases. In Vietnam, RADAR recorded 22 challenges to artistic freedom in 2025, almost double the number documented in 2024. Official Dispatch 69, issued by the Ho Chi Minh City Party Committee’s Propaganda and Mass Mobilization Department in October 2025, called for stricter measures against musical activities showing signs of “deviating from the cultural standard.” Although the dispatch did not formally ban any of the named songs or artists, it triggered a chain of reactions, including the removal of music videos from YouTube by several performers.
Vietnam also saw the targeting of VietPride in 2025. Just two days before its flagship rainbow march in Ho Chi Minh City, VietPride announced the event had been cancelled due to “external reasons.” According to RADAR, at least five other VietPride-related events in the city faced last-minute cancellations or restrictions.
RADAR’s latest report notes that, in 56 percent of cases, works or creators were portrayed as having transgressed imposed boundaries of morality, traditional values or customs, gender, sexuality, or faith, and were subjected to moral policing by state and non-state agents.
“Manufactured conflicts and moral panic over minorities, migrants, and perceived threats to traditional values have put artists at the front line of state and public attacks,” says Kathy Rowland, lead researcher for RADAR.
For artists whose identities and practices already challenge dominant norms, the pressure is intensified. Serena Magiliw, a trans actor and theatre artist from the Philippines, describes how this pressure shapes both her art and her survival.
“It is sad to know that our lives are so intertwined with being policed and surveilled because we are the embodiment of resistance,” she says.
For Magiliw, the struggle is cultural, political, and deeply economic. “I perform for a living. And if I don’t have the space to do that, I won’t survive,” she said. “I can only offer my service, which is art.”
Her words show that moral policing effectively controls whose lives are allowed to be visible, whose histories can be told, and whose futures can be imagined.
Despite these threats, artists continue to persist, finding ingenious ways to build community, extend care, and sustain resilience. Their work reaches beyond survival. It preserves memory and the legacies of hard-fought struggles, reminding new generations on the frontlines of rights movements of the ground that had once been claimed.
Resistance can leave its own mark. In 2025, Filipino drag artist Pura Luka Vega was acquitted by a Manila court of charges related to a 2023 drag performance that prompted an intense backlash from religious groups. The acquittal did not erase the cost of the ordeal, but it offered a hard-won reminder that artists and communities can push back.
In these contexts, artists are often doing work traditionally associated with human rights defenders – but without the same legal, institutional, or community-led support and protection. UAF A&P has recognized this through its Shifting Narratives program, which supports artists and cultural rights workers challenging harmful narratives affecting their communities and connects artist-activists with wider networks of rights defense and community care.
Another artist working within a highly surveilled Southeast Asian state, whose name and identity are being withheld for security and confidentiality, wrote about the relevance of their group’s work in protecting historical legacies from being censored, eradicated and expunged.
“This [work] is also about preserving memory, rather than being entirely dependent on algorithms, censorship, and platform logics. And more importantly, it’s about protecting our labor,” the artist says. “When carefully written and designed work gets deleted without a trace, it’s not just frustrating; it’s one of the reasons many activists feel exhausted. For us, this is also a form of ‘memory infrastructure’ under platform authoritarianism.”
That phrase – memory infrastructure – captures something vital about the role of artists in shrinking civic spaces. In places where public narratives are controlled, archives are fragile, platforms are unpredictable, and dissent is punished, artists help communities remember. They protect stories from disappearance. They create languages for grief, resistance, longing, and survival.
Hope and community are often the only enabling conditions under which most of these artists persist and resist. Yet at a time when all trends point to growing authoritarianism and moral policing in Southeast Asia, and to shrinking tolerance for dissent and minority expressions, art and culture remain the neural systems through which communities preserve and transmit their stories and truths.
When artists are silenced, a community loses one of its ways of imagining, and insisting on, a different future.

articles.title: ASEAN Fractures Widen as Thailand Hosts Myanmar’s Min Aung Hlaing
articles.full_text:
A conversation with Mark Cogan of Kansai Gaidai University in Osaka.
As the people of Myanmar recently commemorated the 8888 uprising that demanded political freedom but was brutally put down in August 1988, Thailand was playing host to Min Aung Hlaing, the former general who seized power through a coup in early 2021.
This was Min Aung Hlaing’s second official visit to an ASEAN member state since military-staged elections in December and January ensured his transition to the presidency and one that widened the schisms within ASEAN, which has barred Myanmar from official summits and events amid a bloody civil war.
Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul broke with that line despite ASEAN protocols and potential legal issues given the International Court of Justice will soon deliver its verdict on whether Min Aung Hlaing and Myanmar’s senior generals committed a genocide against the Rohingya.
Min Aung Hlaing’s first official visit as president was to Laos in early July and his trip to Thailand came less than a week after he allowed a representative from the International Committee of the Red Cross to meet with the jailed former leader Aung San Suu Kyi, who had been unsighted for many years amid concerns for her health.
Mark Cogan is an associate professor of Peace and Conflict Studies at Kansai Gaidai University in Osaka and a regular contributor to The Diplomat. He joined Luke Hunt on Beyond the Mekong to discuss the recent developments in regional politics.
That includes the moral and political questions that have divided maritime and mainland Southeast Asia, including the civil war in Myanmar, which has claimed 100,000 lives, the Code of Conduct in the South China Sea, and Thailand’s simmering border conflict with Cambodia.

articles.title: US Official Reassures Asia of Commitment, Calls for Greater Burden Sharing
articles.full_text:
Undersecretary of War Elbridge Colby told an audience in Manila that U.S. interests are “more engaged than ever in the Indo-Pacific.”
U.S. Under Secretary of War Elbridge Colby speaks at the Ananta Centre in New Delhi, India, Mar. 24, 2026.
The United States remains strongly committed to Asia but wants its partners to bear more of the burden for their own defense, a senior Pentagon official said in the Philippines yesterday.
Seeking to counter concerns about Washington’s reliability, given the capricious character of U.S. foreign policy under the second Trump administration, Undersecretary of War Elbridge Colby said that U.S. interests were “more engaged than ever in the Indo-Pacific.”
“America is definitely not disengaging from Asia,” Colby said in a speech in Manila. “We are not leaving; in fact, we are digging in to ensure a favorable balance of power where it matters most.”
Colby made the remarks at a forum in the Philippines, his first stop on a Southeast Asian tour that will also take him and Assistant Secretary of War John Noh to Indonesia, Thailand, and Cambodia. In a statement, the Department of War said that trip, which will involve meetings with senior officials in each country, “reaffirms the Department’s commitment to build a durable peace in the region through strength.”
During the trip, Colby said in his Manila speech, he intended to “deliver a clear message that is at once both realistic and perhaps bracing but also reassuring: That America’s interests are more engaged than ever in the Indo-Pacific, and that we at the Department of War are concentrated on ensuring those interests are stoutly defended.”
Colby said maintaining a favorable balance of power in the Indo-Pacific required a “posture of deterrence by denial along the First Island Chain,” the barrier of islands that stretches from Japan down to Taiwan, the Philippines, and the northern coast of Borneo.
He pointed to what he said was a growing U.S. military commitment in the region, which has involved the deployment of additional troops, ships, aircraft, and missile systems throughout the First Island Chain. Colby described this as “a formidable, resource-backed posture calibrated to actual structural realities,” contrasting it with the “hollow, merely symbolic engagement of previous decades.”
However, he said that Washington could not manage this itself, and that local partners would need to shoulder more of the burden for their defense.
“When we ask our allies and partners to step up, to invest more in their own defense, and to take responsibility for their own sovereign security, we are not signaling abandonment,” Colby said.
He added, “We are looking for partners, not protectorates.”
The Southeast Asian tour is Colby’s official trip to Southeast Asia as undersecretary of war for policy, and in some ways, it is surprising that it has taken him 18 months to do so. But the intent of yesterday’s speech speaks to an awareness within the Pentagon of the reputational damage that Washington has suffered, in particular due to its indiscriminate tariff policy and misadventure in the Middle East.
Both of these have sent economic reverberations through Asia, and undermined the policy approach preferred by Colby. A hard-nosed realist and advocate of strategic prioritization, he has long advocated a reorientation of U.S. strategic focus from the Middle East toward East Asia, with the goal of preventing China from establishing its hegemony over the region.
While Colby did not explicitly mention China in the speech, his deterrence-focused message is likely to find a receptive audience in parts of the region that face its challenge most acutely. Chief among these is the Philippines, which has recently faced a resumption of China’s maritime pressure campaign in the South China Sea. This culminated in a clash at Second Thomas Shoal in the Spratly Islands on July 20, during which a Philippine sailor sustained a head injury after being struck with a baton by a China Coast Guard member.
Despite its attendant risks, most Southeast Asian governments would prefer the U.S. to maintain a strong presence in Asia, in order to act as a counterweight against China’s growing military power. But security commitments have never been the greatest shortcoming of U.S. policy in Southeast Asia. Indeed, the long-standing complaint is that this is the only thing the U.S. does consistently in the region. This has especially been the case since President Donald Trump’s first electoral victory in 2016, which marked a decisive turn toward economic protectionism and saw the U.S. withdraw from the Trans Pacific Partnership trade pact.
This and the increasingly acrimonious strategic competition with China detracted from the fundamental goals of most governments in the region: trade and economic growth. Despite some stillborn efforts by the Biden administration, such as the Indo-Pacific Economic Framework for Prosperity, these goals have been undermined by much of the agenda of Trump 2.0, in particular the tariffing of close regional partners and allies and the war in Iran, which has led to the blockage of the Strait of Hormuz, through which the region gets a significant proportion of its crude oil.
While the U.S. can help maintain a stable balance of power in Asia, it remains – at least for now – an economically disruptive force on the global stage, to the detriment of its long-term standing in Southeast Asia.

articles.title: Painting Bullseyes: What Iran’s Attacks on US Bases Mean for the Indo-Pacific
articles.full_text:
The attacks in the Middle East have raised anxieties elsewhere, as residents of communities near U.S. bases the world over worry about becoming the target of external aggression.
U.S. Army Soldiers assigned to 4th battalion, 2nd Aviation Regiment, 2nd Combat Aviation Brigade, 2d Infantry Division/ROK-U.S. Combined Division, participate in a field training exercise at Camp Humphreys, South Korea, June 30, 2026.
The United States maintains the world’s largest overseas military basing presence, with as many as 750 installations in 80 countries. Most recently, U.S. bases and bases to which the U.S. military has access in Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates have become the targets of Iranian attacks, in retaliation for U.S. strikes on the country. These attacks have not only resulted in the deaths of several U.S. soldiers, but have impacted local residents in proximity to the bases and pushed others to question the necessity of the U.S. bases entirely. 
Analysts have speculated about what these attacks and the subsequent damages to the bases might mean for U.S. basing in the region, including potential base closures. 
But what does Iran’s targeting of U.S. bases and the resulting destruction mean for the rest of the 80 countries that host the U.S. military? This is an especially salient question for the host countries in the Indo-Pacific, where the specter of a U.S.-China confrontation looms large and U.S. security partners in the region maintain some of the largest troop deployments in the world, with Japan and South Korea hosting the largest and third largest deployments, respectively. 
The attacks in the Middle East have raised anxieties elsewhere, as residents of communities near U.S. bases the world over worry about becoming the target of external aggression. In the wake of Iran’s attacks, for instance, some Philippine policymakers have expressed concerns that by providing the U.S. with basing access, the Philippine government is “effectively painting bullseyes on Filipino soil” vis-à-vis China. 
Such concerns are not new in the Indo-Pacific, although the events in the Middle East may make the prospects of U.S. bases serving as targets more tangible to citizens in the host countries in the region. Peace and anti-base activists have long claimed that one potential negative externality for the communities hosting U.S. bases is that the bases and the community surrounding them may be targeted by U.S. enemies or those of the host nation. 
In Okinawa, Japan, for example, peace activists have argued that the disproportionately large U.S. base presence in the prefecture would make Okinawa “the first place for an enemy to attack.” This narrative has only grown louder as tensions between the U.S. and China, particularly over the nearby Taiwan Strait, have increased. In South Korea, one of the concerns regarding the installation of the Terminal High Altitude Area Defense system in 2017 was that it would make the host village of Soseong “one of the first targets of attack” if there was conflict between the U.S. and North Korea and/or China. 
Narratives that describe the U.S. bases as dangerous to the communities which host them are part of the wider non-in-my-backyard (NIMBY) phenomenon that several scholars have noted. While citizens in the countries that host U.S. bases may generally support their country’s security alliance with the U.S., they are typically more reticent to bear the burdens of the potential negative consequences of the bases by hosting them in their community. Other potential NIMBY-related consequences range from accidents and crimes related to the U.S. troop presence to environmental degradation such as per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances contamination and more quotidian issues such as base-related traffic jams and noise pollution. As with the narratives claiming that hosting a U.S. military presence will make the community a potential target of an external attack, peace and anti-base activists draw attention to these potential negative externalities as well. When activists characterize the U.S. military presence in ways that are more tangible to citizens, such as these NIMBY-related issues, they tend to be more effective at rallying anti-base protests than, for example, making pacifist and nationalistic claims.
Of course, activists’ messages and even anti-U.S.-base protests do not directly translate into general public opinion about hosting U.S. military bases. A 14-country survey administered in the 2010s found that citizens in most of these U.S. base-hosting countries had mostly positive or neutral opinions about the U.S. military presence in their country. The four host countries in the Indo-Pacific included in the study (Australia, Japan, the Philippines, and South Korea) were no different, with 76 percent of Filipino respondents having very or somewhat favorable attitudes (the highest of the 14 countries), 52 percent in South Korea, and 50 percent in Australia. The rate was just 34 percent in Japan, but this was still higher than the neutral and very or somewhat unfavorable attitudes among Japanese respondents. 
A larger survey conducted this year after the onset of the U.S.-Israel-Iran conflict paints perhaps a more sobering picture, with respondents in most U.S. host countries in the survey having a net negative opinion of hosting U.S. troops. However, in these same Indo-Pacific host countries, arguably the key U.S. security partners in the region, public opinion about the U.S. bases remains among the highest, with South Korea and Japan recording net 14 and net 2 positive opinions of hosting U.S. bases, respectively. Respondents in the Philippines (-2) and Australia (-18) held more positive or undecided views combined than negative ones.
Taken together these patterns reveal a few points about what is happening in the Indo-Pacific host countries regarding protests against and public opinion about U.S. military bases following the onset of the conflict in Iran and Iran’s retaliatory attacks on U.S. installations in the region. 
First, peace activists in the Indo-Pacific, and likely in other regions outside the Middle East such as Europe, will increasingly problematize the U.S. bases as “drawing a target” on the base-hosting communities. As a scholar who recently conducted fieldwork on anti-U.S.-base activism in South Korea, I heard this narrative from several activists. 
Second, this framing may be convincing to host nation citizens, as the recent attacks on the bases in the Middle East show that this threat is both credible and tangible. 
Even if this framing has become more convincing, it may not necessarily translate into more support for the withdrawal of U.S. troops in these Indo-Pacific host countries or closure of U.S. bases. However, this may be a bigger concern for Indo-Pacific countries which are trying to be politically and militarily equidistant from both the U.S. and China, in the event of a militarized conflict between the two superpowers. Additionally, as relayed to me by one interviewee, it may increase public support for developing indigenous military capability, including nuclear weapons, even for long-time U.S. allies.
The United States maintains the world’s largest overseas military basing presence, with as many as 750 installations in 80 countries. This is an especially salient question for the host countries in the Indo-Pacific, where the specter of a U.S.-China confrontation looms large and U.S. security partners in the region maintain some of the largest troop deployments in the world, with Japan and South Korea hosting the largest and third largest deployments, respectively.

In the wake of Iran’s attacks, for instance, some Philippine policymakers have expressed concerns that by providing the U.S. with basing access, the Philippine government is “effectively painting bullseyes on Filipino soil” vis-à-vis China.

Peace and anti-base activists have long claimed that one potential negative externality for the communities hosting U.S. bases is that the bases and the community surrounding them may be targeted by U.S. enemies or those of the host nation. 
In Okinawa, Japan, for example, peace activists have argued that the disproportionately large U.S. base presence in the prefecture would make Okinawa “the first place for an enemy to attack.” This narrative has only grown louder as tensions between the U.S. and China, particularly over the nearby Taiwan Strait, have increased. articles.title: Air Force Ascendant: Senior PLA Leadership Changes and Their Implications
articles.full_text:
If current trends continue, the PLAAF is likely going to have a greater-than-usual presence on the next Central Military Commission.
Chinese airmen parade during a full honors arrival ceremony at the Ministry of National Defense headquarters in Beijing, China, July 12, 2000.
Amid leadership disruption caused by the purges, the reconstruction of the People’s Liberation Army’s (PLA) high command is underway. Recent reports by the South China Morning Post and Channel News Asia indicate that officers from the PLA Air Force (PLAAF) have recently risen to senior leadership positions, prompting renewed discussions on the significance of this development. 
At present, PLAAF officers are in charge of five Central Military Commission (CMC) departments, compared with seven headed by Army officers, making the PLAAF the second-best-represented service at the CMC level. Moreover, of the PLA’s five theater commands, PLAAF officers lead two: the Eastern and Central Theater Commands. Meanwhile, an Army lieutenant general heads the Northern Theater Command, while a Navy vice admiral leads the Southern Theater Command. The situation within the Western Theater Command is murkier. Its commander, an Army general, has been missing for many months and his PLAAF deputy appears to have taken up some of his responsibilities. 
Overall, the expanding PLAAF presence at the top of the PLA hierarchy is obvious. If current trends continue, the PLAAF is likely going to have a greater-than-usual presence on the next CMC, whose composition is expected to be confirmed at the 21st  Party Congress in 2027. This development has the potential to reshape the PLA in multiple ways, rendering an analysis of the PLAAF’s rise and its wider implications worthy. 
The PLAAF’s representation on the CMC has historically been limited. In the Xi Jinping era, only two PLAAF officers served as CMC members: PLAAF Commander Ma Xiaotian from 2012 to 2017, and Air Force General Xu Qiliang as the CMC vice chairman from 2012 to 2022. Only one PLAAF officer served as the director of a CMC department: Air Force General Xu Xueqiang, who led the Equipment Development Department from 2022 until 2026. 
However, the limited representation may have been a blessing in disguise. As officers from other services rose to prominence, many quickly became targets of the expanding purges. With few senior leaders at high posts, the PLAAF was less exposed to the turbulence. From 2013 to 2026, there were only ten documented cases of senior PLAAF officers falling victim to the purges, with the most recent cases being the aforementioned Xu Xueqiang and the PLAAF’s 14th Political Commissar Guo Puxiao. 
The survival of PLAAF officers provided Xi with a larger pool of candidates to draw upon as he seeks to rebuild the PLA’s senior leadership. Also, PLAAF officers’ ability to survive constant Discipline Inspection Commission surveillance may have strengthened Xi’s confidence in their reliability. The rise of PLAAF officers is therefore natural in a time of leadership reconstruction amid elevating global tensions, creating a situation where military talents are desperately needed.  
The rise of PLAAF officers to senior leadership posts could influence future PLA development in several ways. As PLAAF officers gain more say, they are likely to advocate for their service and specialties. At CMC meetings, they are certain to promote the importance of air power, which has proved to be critical in recent conflicts. At the beginning of the Iran War, U.S. and Israeli air superiority enabled the decapitation of Iran’s civilian and military leadership. However, vulnerabilities in U.S. and Gulf states’ air defenses subsequently shifted the initiative and drained U.S. stocks of critical interceptors. The conflict highlighted the need to invest resources to improve offensive and defensive capabilities in the air domain.
PLAAF officers could cite these examples to advocate for more investment in air defense systems, unmanned aerial vehicles, counter-drone technologies, air base protection, and munitions production. Such investments could benefit the PLA, since China’s next war will likely require extensive air force participation. The recent revelation of the air-launched, nuclear-capable JL-1 missile on board the H-6N bomber may reflect China’s intent to strengthen and expand its air force capabilities. 
A stronger emphasis on air power will divert more resources to the PLAAF. Yet, an unintended consequence might be resource competition with the traditionally powerful Army, whose personnel constitute nearly half of the PLA and occupy a majority of senior leadership posts. Xi cannot afford to alienate the Army, which remains the bedrock of the armed forces and essential to regime security. Looking ahead, Xi is likely to use his personal authority as CMC chairman to mitigate possible tensions between the ascendant airmen and still-dominant army officers, with the ultimate goal being achieving greater jointness across the services. 
As Xi constructs a new generation of PLA leaders, he seems to favor a team with a significant number of PLAAF officers. This development could benefit PLA capabilities by giving more institutional weight to air power, when its relevance to military success has been made evident through recent conflicts. Nonetheless, one should expect politics to overshadow officer selection and promotion, as this has always been the case with the PLA. 
In the Xi era, the PLA has experienced considerable instability due to the anti-corruption campaign. There is no guarantee that the now favored PLAAF officers will not fall prey to the rolling purges, despite their previous experience as the least affected service. Ultimately, the past has shown that the higher PLA officers move up in the chain of command, the greater scrutiny they face, as they become enmeshed in an environment of mistrust. In essence, one must not disregard the influence of politics when analyzing the trajectory of PLA developments.  
There may be a short period of unity among senior PLA leaders after the 21st Party Congress. However, if recurring dynamics of the Xi era endure, instability could reemerge once again to disrupt PLA capability, even undermining the careers of PLAAF officers who are currently on the ascent.

articles.title: Safeguarding Storage: Wildberries’ Move to Kazakhstan
articles.full_text:
As drone strikes on Wildberries warehouses across Russia continue, the company moves to increase its presence in Kazakhstan
On August 4, Kazakhstani Minister for Trade and Integration Arman Shakkaliyev announced that the Russian e-commerce platform Wildberries would expand its warehouse capacity in the country. According to the minister, Wildberries plans to build 260,000 square meters of storage, split between Astana and Almaty, expanding its capacity more than eightfold from its current 46,000 square meters of leased warehouse space. 
The announcement comes following a July marked by more than 20 attacks on Wildberries’ logistical hubs across Russia, also affecting Kazakh sellers on the platform who have lost an estimated $3.2 million worth of goods.
Despite media reports framing the expansion as a relocation of the e-commerce platform, the planned warehouses in Kazakhstan would not be able to cover the more than 1 million square meters lost over the last month. On top of this, Wildberries’ new warehouses planned in Kazakhstan are, at the time of writing, only set to be completed in 2027, thereby not solving the current problems facing the company. This news, however, came just days after the Russian newspaper cited multiple sources saying the company was looking for 100,000 square meters of extra storage.
Wildberries’ overall aim to build more warehouses in Kazakhstan is not new. In fact, such an effort announced at the beginning of 2023, with plans to open two years later before the project was postponed. The company’s market share in Kazakhstan has grown, now making it a distant second with almost 27 percent of the e-commerce market. Locally founded Kaspi keeps almost two-thirds of the market.
Wildberries is reportedly scrambling to find an additional 100,000 square meters of warehouse space as a result of the last month’s many attacks. Reports of this new search for space came as it became clear that losses at Wildberries hubs in Russia could amount to upward of $3.37 billion.
With losses from Kazakh vendors alone exceeding $3 million, Shakkaliyev, during the announcement of Wildberries’ construction plan, urged Kazakh citizens to use local e-commerce platforms like Kaspi rather than foreign alternatives, both for selling and buying goods.
“We must use our domestic marketplaces. We call this economic patriotism. We currently have a very high share of domestic marketplaces, so, of course, we should try to order locally,” the minister said, stating that only through these channels could people be guaranteed that their products were delivered.
This statement is just one sign that the role of Wildberries in Kazakhstan, and Central Asia in general, could be challenged by the recent attacks. Even before this advice was given, Kyrgyz clothing manufacturers showed interest in replacing Wildberries with Kazakh platforms, both due to financial interest and the protection of the stored inventory.
Likewise, Kazakh sellers have taken into consideration using local platforms from either Kazakhstan or a larger market like Uzbekistan. A central issue for some of the sellers was, however, access to the much larger Russian market.
New warehouses could become key for Wildberries going forward for reasons beyond keeping its market share. According to a Kommersant report, for example, expansion of the e-commerce company’s Kazakh operations was linked to wishes of protecting some of its goods, rather than just local expansion. By constructing warehouses in Kazakhstan and neighboring Uzbekistan, Wildberries could safeguard parts of its inventory and some of the losses it has taken over the past month.
Similar measures were taken in early August by competing Russian e-commerce platform OZON, which focused on moving expensive goods away from more easily targetable logistical hubs.
While the future opening of new logistical hubs might increase Wildberries’ importance in Kazakhstan, it does not seem likely to safeguard the company as a whole. Instead, what will be relevant is what the Russian e-commerce heavyweight decides to put in these new Central Asian warehouses and what the state of the company will be at that time.
